news.title: Kamala Harris becomes a campaign trail dilemma for Democrats in key midterm races
news.text:
Harris lost Alaska to President Donald Trump by 13 points in 2024, underscoring the political challenge for Democrats running in the state.

Other Democrats running in red-leaning states did not seem receptive to support from Harris.

ROB SAND AND JOSH TUREK DON’T WANT KAMALA HARRIS TO CAMPAIGN FOR THEM IN IOWA

A campaign spokesperson for Rob Sand, the Democratic gubernatorial nominee in Iowa, told the Washington Examiner that the campaign does not want an endorsement from Harris, nor do they want her to appear at any campaign rallies or have any involvement with Sand’s campaign. The position marks a stark contrast with 2018, when Harris supported Sand’s successful campaign for Iowa state auditor. Trump carried Iowa by 13.2 points over Harris in 2024.

This week, the Cook Political Report moved the Iowa gubernatorial race from “toss-up” to “leans Democratic.” It also changed Iowa’s Senate race from “leans Republican” to “toss-up” — a boost to Democratic Senate candidate Josh Turek.

Iowa Democrats appear to be on the cusp of reviving their base after the Cook Political Report recently changed its rating of the Iowa gubernatorial race from “toss-up” to “leans Democratic.” It also changed Iowa’s Senate race from “leans Republican” to “toss-up” — a boost to Democrat Josh Turek.

Turek’s campaign told the Washington Examiner he has no plans to campaign with Harris and isn’t seeking her support. In 2024, Turek, an Iowa state representative, outperformed Harris by roughly 13 points in his district, illustrating the dramatically different political coalitions the two Democrats assembled in Iowa.

University of Iowa political scientist Timothy Hagle noted in an interview that Republicans hold a roughly 190,000-voter registration advantage in the state, a gap that has grown over the last several election cycles.

“We have an open Senate seat, an open governor’s race, and I think that the nominees in those races and sort of a lot of Iowa Democrats more generally sort of understand they don’t want to spoil that by appearing to be too far to the left on issues,” Hagle said. “And so if they were to associate with Kamala Harris, it could be a problem for them.”

The distancing from Harris in red states isn’t new for Democrats.

In one of her forays back into the political scene after the 2024 loss, Harris visited Tennessee in November 2025 for her 107 Days book tour but did not explicitly endorse or even mention state Rep. Aftyn Behn, who was then running for the state’s 7th Congressional District, by name. At an event where Harris and Behn both appeared, the lawmaker left before Harris arrived, citing a fundraiser she needed to attend.

But not all Democrats are running away from Harris.

Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-GA) held a private “Women for Ossoff” call with Harris, where he said it was a “delight” to see her. Ossoff is running in one of the most closely watched Senate battles. But unlike Democrats running in red-leaning states, Georgia has become a perennial purple state that Democrats must keep if they hope to regain control of the upper chamber.

The Peach State is also home to a sizable black electorate, a constituency Democratic strategist Dallas Jones identified as one of Harris’s remaining strengths within the Democratic coalition.

A spokesperson for the Ossoff campaign told the Washington Examiner that “Senator Ossoff is grateful for Vice President Harris’ help and support in his re-election campaign.”

In addition to Ossoff, the former vice president endorsed Senate Democratic candidates including Troy Jackson in Maine, Abdul el Sayed in Michigan, Roy Cooper in North Carolina, and James Talarico in Texas. It is not clear whether Harris has endorsed former Ohio Sen. Sherrod Brown’s comeback bid against Sen. Jon Husted (R-OH). The Brown campaign did not respond to a request for comment from the Washington Examiner.

Jones said that while Harris’s endorsement still carries real weight, it’s mainly only on two fronts.

“It’s base energy and money, and so fundraising, her list, and donor networks are still strong in the party,” said Jones. “And so sometimes that comes in with a bump in small-dollar money. Base turnout, especially with black voters, women, younger progressives, she still remains a trusted messenger.”

Among the potential 2028 Democratic candidates, Harris continues to poll in first place. A recent Focaldata-Financial Times poll showed that Harris received 30% support, more than double her closest competitor, Gov. Gavin Newsom (D-CA), at 14%. Simply ignoring Harris may not be prudent for Democrats. Harris still has loyal followers in the party who claim her truncated 107-day race against Trump, after Biden dropped out, did not give her sufficient time to run a serious campaign.

Harris’s standing creates a complicated dynamic for Democrats. She remains one of the party’s most recognizable figures and retains a national fundraising network and loyal base of supporters, even as candidates in Republican-leaning states appear wary of associating themselves too closely with the former vice president.

“Now, in the case of Mary Peltola, in some of the places that are more conservative, where they are polling well, they still need Republicans to swing the pendulum and to get them over the hump,” Jones added. “So a rejection of a Kamala Harris endorsement makes sense in those states as a campaign strategy.”

Harris has not held a public campaign rally with a Democratic candidate since appearing in Tennessee during Behn’s unsuccessful congressional campaign, although that could change before November.

SOUTH CAROLINA’S MOVE TO FRONT OF 2028 DEMOCRATIC PRIMARY CALENDAR COULD BENEFIT KAMALA HARRIS

Hagle said Harris’s struggles as the Democratic nominee in 2024 could help explain why some candidates are reluctant to put her on the campaign trail.

“She was not a great candidate in terms of a lot of her public appearances and things and statements that she made, being criticized for having word salad and things of that nature, and so it was just too easy for the Republicans to poke fun at that,” Hagle said. “But she can speak to her supporters in a way that would maybe get them energized, and that’s kind of the key: is if you can get your base energized, that can be important.”
news.summary: Democrats running in competitive races this midterm cycle are grappling with how to handle former Vice President Kamala Harris on the campaign trail, with some candidates welcoming her help while others are keeping their distance. Harris remains a front-runner for the 2028 Democratic presidential nomination, but her ties to the Biden administration and 2024 loss […]

news.title: Rubio holds advantage over Vance in matchups against Democratic presidential candidates - poll
news.text: Secretary of State Marco Rubio currently holds an advantage over Vice President JD Vance in hypothetical matchups against several potential Democratic presidential candidates in the 2028 election, according to an Emerson College poll released over the weekend.According to the poll, Rubio defeats both former vice president Kamala Harris and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez in hypothetical races by the same margin, 48% to 43%. Vance, by comparison, narrowly defeats Ocasio-Cortez, 46% to 44%, but loses to Harris by four percentage points.California Gov. Gavin Newsom performs better than both leading Republican figures in the poll, leading Vance 49% to 44% and Rubio 48% to 46%. The two Democrats showing the strongest results against the two Republicans are former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg and Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff. Buttigieg leads both Rubio and Vance by 49% to 44%, while Ossoff leads Rubio 47% to 44% and Vance 49% to 44%.The findings are particularly notable amid questions over who could succeed US President Donald Trump as the Republican nominee. Rubio has already said he would not run for the nomination in 2028 if Vance decides to enter the race, while Vance has said he will make a decision after the November midterm elections.Trump told donors to choose JD Vance for next presidentThe Washington Post reported earlier this month that Trump told donors in private conversations that “ultimately, we need to choose JD,” but later publicly qualified his remarks, saying it was too early to discuss endorsing a candidate. Trump has also previously suggested that Vance and Rubio run together, calling them a “dream team,” without saying which of the two should lead the ticket.The poll was conducted on August 16-17 among 1,000 registered voters, with a margin of error of three percentage points. This means that some of the closer gaps, including Newsom's lead over Rubio, fall within the margin of error and should not be viewed at this early stage as predictions of the outcome of the 2028 election.

news.title: Stop blaming corruption. Washington’s real problem is basic arithmetic
news.text:
The mathematics show that personal representation of every citizen is impossible. No elected official, regardless of talent or dedication, possesses sufficient time to know hundreds of thousands — let alone millions — of individual constituents. Modern representative government must then rely upon institutions, staff, committees, bureaucracies, political parties, and systems that compress millions of individual voices into collective decisions.

Our country started off much smaller. The first constitutional census in 1790 recorded a population of just under 4 million people. Following that census and the resulting apportionment, there were 105 members of the House of Representatives and 26 senators, along with a president and vice president — a total of 133 elected federal officials. A member of the House represented approximately 37,000 citizens. Across the federal government as a whole, there was roughly one elected federal official for every 29,500 Americans. Today, each elected federal official corresponds, on average, to roughly 650,000 citizens, with the average House district ballooning to over 760,000 residents. This shift was not merely an accident of demographic growth but a choice of policy. When Congress passed the Permanent Apportionment Act of 1929, it limited the House of Representatives to 435 members. As the American population has expanded, the number of representatives has effectively stood still. The practical experience of representation has not.

This shows the first limit of representation within the government. As populations expand and structural limits remain in place, each citizen’s share of representative attention declines. This is not the result of corruption, incompetence, or malice. It is the unavoidable math of governing a nation of hundreds of millions of citizens. The result is individuals having less representational value while the government continues to exert more control over the individual.

Representative attention has another consequence. Whenever a valuable resource becomes scarce, competition inevitably follows. In politics, that scarce resource is the attention of elected officials. Individual citizens possess an equal constitutional claim to representation, yet they compete with organizations capable of aggregating thousands or even millions of voices into a single, persistent message. Lobbyists, labor unions, advocacy groups, and industry organizations do not create this competition — they are products of it.

A professional lobbyist’s purpose is to secure and maintain the attention of government. In a system where representative attention is necessarily finite, a lobbyist will almost invariably receive more representative attention — and therefore more practical representation — than an individual citizen acting alone. We know American federalism was designed to distribute representative responsibility among local, state, and federal governments. However, as federal authority has expanded into daily civic life, the strain on those 537 federal offices has only intensified, leaving citizens increasingly reliant on the very layer of government least capable of providing individualized representative attention.

This shows a second limit of representation — one that flows directly from the first but cannot be measured mathematically. Because representatives cannot maintain a direct feedback loop with millions of constituents, power inevitably shifts to intermediary systems: party leaders, committee structures, legislative staff, and administrative apparatuses. As these institutional buffers grow, the distance widens between the vote a citizen casts and the political outcome that follows.

Representation depends not only upon the capacity of government to hear us but also upon the continuity between the vote we cast and the government that ultimately acts in our name. If a ballot is disconnected from the decision it was intended to influence, something vital is lost. The legal process may remain intact, yet the individual citizen experiences a diminished sense of representation. How many people feel this way in today’s America?

Recent political events illustrate this philosophical tension. During the 2024 Democratic presidential primaries, millions of voters cast ballots for delegates pledged to former President Joe Biden. After Biden withdrew from the race, those delegates ultimately nominated then-Vice President Kamala Harris in accordance with established party procedures. Whether one approves or disapproves of that outcome is not the point; the convention acted strictly within its rules. The deeper question is philosophical rather than legal. When citizens cast votes expecting to influence one specific outcome, but subsequent institutional processes produce another, how can we understand the practical value of their vote? The same question arises whenever election machinery falters, whenever ballots are improperly counted, or whenever citizens conclude that their participation no longer influences outcomes in the way they were promised. Representation is not merely a legal status. It is a relationship between citizen and government — one that depends heavily upon both legitimacy and trust.

This brings us back to the original question. What is your vote worth? That is for you to decide.

IF YOU WON’T FACE VOTERS, DON’T ASK FOR THEIR VOTE

Your vote is also your claim upon a government’s finite capacity for representative attention. Its value depends not only upon equal access to the ballot box but also upon the extent to which that claim remains meaningfully connected to the governmental decisions that follow.

Democracy promises every citizen an equal right to participate. It cannot promise unlimited representative attention, nor can it guarantee that every citizen will always feel personally represented. Representation is bounded by two unavoidable realities: finite representative attention and the philosophical continuity between choice and outcome. Perhaps the question is not whether democracy represents us equally. The Constitution answers that. The more difficult question is how much representative attention any one of us can realistically possess in a nation of 349 million citizens. Until we begin asking that question, we may continue confusing the promise of equal representation with the practical limits of representation itself.

Andrew Moore is a small-business owner and author of the Primus Aeternus series.
news.summary: Five hundred thirty-seven elected federal officials are responsible for approximately 349 million Americans. That seems more than fair, doesn’t it? The Constitution guarantees every citizen an equal claim to representation, but it does not tell us how much representation that claim can realistically provide. It is a mathematical and philosophical question, not constitutional. Representation is […]

news.title: Mixed support from black voters threatens el Sayed’s Michigan Senate hopes
news.text:
That result leaves el Sayed with an immediate challenge: winning back voters who could have supported him in the primary but chose someone else.

He has seemingly yet to develop an answer to his problem. When asked how he would respond to black voters who do not support him, el Sayed pointed to his own African identity rather than directly addressing why those voters might be skeptical of his candidacy.

Irina Tsukerman, a political analyst and president of Scarab Rising, said the response was awkward because black Americans and African immigrants can have distinct political histories and experiences.

“His answer about his African identity was awkward because it did not address what black voters were actually asking,” Tsukerman told the Washington Examiner.

El Sayed’s primary coalition was strongest among younger and progressive voters, who tend to be predominantly white, while Stevens performed better among black, older, and metro Detroit voters. A July Glengariff Group survey similarly found Stevens leading among black voters, while el Sayed performed better among younger, white, and outstate voters.

“El Sayed’s weakness with black voters is serious, but black voters are not a political group chat,” Nick E. Smith, a Democratic strategist and president of Polaris, told the Washington Examiner. “Age, ideology, income and geography matter.”

Smith said el Sayed’s Wayne County loss should be viewed as a warning sign despite his previous government position there.

“Having the resume doesn’t mean you have the relationship,” Smith said. “Voters weren’t handing out extra credit for previous employment.”

Some black Democrats are now openly withholding support or opposing el Sayed, raising questions about whether he can broaden his coalition before facing Republican Mike Rogers in November.

Rogers appears to be seizing on el Sayed’s struggles. On Thursday, the Republican nominee launched a “Democrats for Rogers” coalition featuring state Rep. Karen Whitsett, a conservative-leaning Democrat who said she’d support Rogers in the fall.

El Sayed’s struggle with black voters is not necessarily driven by a single issue. El Sayed’s support for the Uncommitted movement during the 2024 Democratic presidential primary remains a point of tension, particularly among voters who believed defeating President Donald Trump should have been the overriding priority. Detroit journalist Orlando Bailey recently said black voters remain “holding his feet to the fire” over that record.

But analysts caution against reducing the problem entirely to Israel and Gaza.

Voters in Detroit, Tsukerman said, are more likely to be looking for answers about jobs, schools, housing, crime, health care, small businesses, and economic opportunity — as well as whether black political leaders and communities will influence him.

“Pointing to his African background answers a question about his own identity rather than their political concerns,” Tsukerman said.

The stakes are heightened by a new AARP poll showing el Sayed leading Rogers by just 1 point, 48%-47%, with 5% undecided. El Sayed performs better among younger voters and women, while Rogers leads among older voters and men.

A separate Fox News poll conducted earlier in August found Rogers leading el Sayed 51% to 47%, while el Sayed held a 75% to 22% advantage among black voters. The differing results underscore the fluidity of the early general-election environment.

Former Vice President Kamala Harris, who struggled in parts of Wayne County such as Dearborn over concerns about Gaza, won black voters in Michigan, 87%-11%, according to CNN exit polling in 2024. She won Wayne County by 29 points; meanwhile, Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-MI) won Wayne County by 32 points over Rogers.

But Rogers’ lead with older voters could compound el Sayed’s challenge with black voters.

“Rogers is stronger with older voters; el Sayed with younger voters,” Smith said. “Young voters bring energy. Older voters have the annoying habit of actually showing up for midterms. In a 48%-47% race, that matters.”

Tsukerman said the greatest danger for Democrats may not be black voters switching to Rogers, but simply deciding not to turn out.

“Rogers does not need thousands of black Democrats to vote for him,” she said. “He benefits if they simply decide they are not interested enough in el Sayed to vote in the Senate race.”

That could be consequential given how narrowly Rogers lost his previous Senate bid.

In 2024, Slotkin defeated Rogers by 19,006 votes, 48.6% to 48.3%. Even a relatively small decline in Democratic turnout in Detroit and Wayne County could alter the electoral math this time around.

“Several thousand fewer Democratic votes in Detroit, accompanied by relatively small Republican gains elsewhere, can erase a margin of that size,” Tsukerman said.

Jeff Burton, a former deputy executive director of the National Republican Congressional Committee and cofounding partner at Maven Advocacy, said el Sayed’s coalition has vulnerabilities beyond black voters, including Jewish voters and union households.

“El Sayed can excite younger progressives and Arab American voters, but they cannot replace black voters in Detroit, Jewish voters, and union households increasingly willing to vote Republican,” Burton told the Washington Examiner.

He cautioned that the broader political environment could ultimately determine how damaging those weaknesses prove to be.

“In a neutral political environment, those weaknesses could make him unelectable,” Burton said. “If the economy remains voters’ overriding concern, however, it may be the one issue big enough to paper over all of them.”

Democrats argue that Rogers has significant vulnerabilities of his own.

“There is no question this will be a tight election,” Democratic strategist Joe Caiazzo told the Washington Examiner. “However, Rogers has to defend the unpopular policies of Trump and MAGA Republicans that have led to this affordability crisis for Michiganders and all Americans.”

Republicans, Caiazzo said, will try to frame the race around el Sayed’s ideology rather than the economy.

For el Sayed, however, the challenge is that he cannot simply assume traditional Democratic voters will return to the party’s nominee in November.

“Neither party has a lifetime subscription to the black vote,” Smith said. “El Sayed’s younger, progressive and Arab American supporters can expand his coalition, but they can’t replace older black and other traditional Democratic voters.”

ABDUL EL SAYED OUTPERFORMS MIKE ROGERS IN LATEST MICHIGAN SENATE POLL

El Sayed now has to campaign on two fronts: persuading independents and suburban voters who may be skeptical of a progressive nominee, while rebuilding relationships with Democratic voters who already had a chance to choose him and declined.

“El Sayed can’t assume black voters who rejected him in the primary will return simply because there’s a ‘D’ next to his name,” Smith said. “He still has to earn the vote.”
news.summary: Abdul el Sayed is contending with the fact that the Democratic Party’s most reliable voters could cost him the election in the high-stakes matchup with former Rep. Mike Rogers for Michigan’s Senate race. Black voters have helped propel his party to statewide victories for years, but they were significantly less enthusiastic about his candidacy than […]
news.author: Barnini Chakraborty

news.title: Barabak: Ripple or blue wave? This race will test Democratic strength in November
news.text: The high desert is not typically a place you look for a wave. But in the vast expanse between the Sierra Nevada and Utah border, a not-exactly-wide-open race for Congress is testing whether a blue wave, should one come November, is ankle-high or something more akin to a political tsunami. Nevada's 2nd District has been represented by just four lawmakers since its creation more than 40 years ago. All those representatives have been Republicans. November's contest should be another shoo-in for the GOP and its nominee, David Flippo. The district, which takes in northern Nevada, is overwhelmingly white and rural, which makes it solidly conservative. In 2024, Donald Trump beat Kamala Harris by a decisive 56% to 42%; only Washoe County, home to Reno, kept things that close. Trump won other portions of the district by 50 percentage points or more. But inflation, Trump's sagging approval rating and other factors — northern resentment toward southern Nevada, where Flippo lived until fairly recently, the refusal of the incumbent to support his party's nominee — offer Democrats the not-entirely-far-fetched hope of a major upset. "It will be an interesting summer and fall," Mark Amodei, who has represented the district for 15 years, wrote on social media after the June primary. "But I believe it’s fair to say that CD-2, for the first time in its history, isn’t a Republican guarantee." That's just about the kindest thing the congressman has had to say about his would-be successor. All of which make the sprawling district in Nevada's rough and rocky Great Basin an improbable political bellwether. A win on such forbidding terrain would almost certainly mean a nationwide Democratic gain of 30 or more seats in November; they need to flip just three to take control of the House. Flippo, 63, a 25-year Air Force veteran and Trump stalwart, arrived in the district from Las Vegas. He ran for Congress there in 2024, losing in the Republican primary. He was preparing for a second try in the Democratic-leaning 4th District when Amodei unexpectedly announced his retirement in February. So Flippo hightailed it north to run in the far more hospitable 2nd District. He took on the favored candidate of Amodei and others in the GOP establishment, James Settelmeyer, a former minority leader of the state Senate. Backed by a constellation of MAGA celebrities, Flippo waged a fiercely negative campaign, accusing "Tampon Jim" of voting to put menstrual products in boys' bathrooms and coddling undocumented immigrants, among other distortions. With Trump's endorsement, Flippo handily defeated Settelmeyer and 11 other primary opponents. ""Absolutely scurrilous campaign against ... one of the nicest guys around," Amodei said afterward, on the program "Nevada Newsmakers." "The voters are never wrong. But guess what? Mark Amodei’s not endorsing [Flippo.] I wish him all the best. No way. No, thank you.” Apart from his exceedingly short-term residency in the district, questions have also been raised about Flippo's opaque finances. He has lent his campaign more than $1.6 million and failed to provide the personal disclosure information required of federal candidates. There is also no record of Flippo filing the required statement during his 2024 campaign, according to the Washington news outlet NOTUS. In addition, it reported that Flippo was fired from a job in the financial services industry after his company accused him of violating policies and regulations. So, a carpetbagger with a sketchy history. Flippo's main opponent is Teresa Benitez-Thompson, 48, a longtime Reno resident, former member of the state Assembly and a relatively moderate Democrat. Those credentials also buoy Democratic hopes. The party’s congressional campaign committee has, for the first time in decades, added Nevada’s 2nd District to its target list, though it remains to be seen how much time and money national Democrats commit to the race. To prevail, Benitez-Thompson would have to defy political gravity, which is to say overcome the reflexive partisanship that has typified politics in this age of deep voter polarization. In the last two midterm elections, according to the Pew Research Center, more than 90% of Republican and Republican-leaning voters supported GOP candidates for the House. In other words, the kind of crossover voters that Benitez-Thompson needs to win have become rare indeed. "“Trump is a huge liability for Republicans; there is no question that the GOP is going to have huge turnout problems, meaning that in a lot of races, Democrats are going to greatly exceed expectations," the veteran election handicapper Charlie Cook wrote in a recent midterm analysis. "But converting Republican voters to actually back a Democrat — even for a day — is so much harder now." Jon Ralston, one of Nevada's leading political savants, agreed. "Some of those rural Nevada voters would rather commit hara-kiri than vote for a Democrat," Ralston said. (No, Japan's ancient suicide ritual is not particularly associated with honor or custom in the cow counties, as Nevada's lightly populated stretches are known. But you get the point.) "I don't think it's impossible," Ralston, founder and chief executive of the Nevada Independent news site, said of a Democratic upset. "But I remain skeptical." Here's the thing, though, about wave elections — and, to be clear, your friendly political columnist is offering no predictions ahead of November. Like a massive ocean swell, which can bear all kinds of flotsam and jetsam ashore, a political wave that is big enough, broad enough and strong enough can carry all manner of unlikely candidates to victory. Even in the bone-dry desert.
news.summary: The contest in Nevada's 2nd Congressional District should be a shoo-in for Republicans. But a problematic candidate, inflation and Trump's unpopularity give Democrats not far-fetched hopes for a massive upset.
news.author: Mark Z. Barabak

news.title: Bill Maher blasts Democratic Party, says it is fine with religion ‘as long as that faith isn’t Jewish’
news.text:
Comedian Bill Maher took aim at what he portrayed as the Democratic Party’s double standard on religion Friday, quipping that a candidate’s public faith is welcome “as long as that faith isn’t Jewish.”

The segment aired after CNN anchor Dana Bash discussed Texas Democrat James Talarico’s outspoken Christianity during a segment on “Real Time,” saying he “wears his faith on his sleeve” in a way Talarico believes could help him.

“Well, in the Democratic Party, as long as that faith isn’t Jewish, you’re good,” Maher retorted.

“Well, you said it.” Bash replied.

Maher then interjected, “Yeah, I said it because it’s true!”

Pew Research Center polling shows 80% of Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents (80%) hold an unfavorable view of Israel, up sharply from 53% in 2022.

At the same time, 41% of Republicans and Republican-leaning independents surveyed hold a negative view of the Jewish state.

Fifty-eight percent of those right-leaning voters have a positive view. 

The Democratic Party has also put forth a series of candidates, personalities and elected officials who espouse anti-Israel beliefs, including Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. 

Far-left Twitch streamer Hasan Piker has repeatedly criticized Israel.

When reached for comment Saturday, Sam Markstein, Republican Jewish Coalition national political director and spokesman, agreed with Maher and spoke of the GOP as the only party still willing to accommodate Jewish people who are proud of their identity and support of Israel.

“It’s a rare occasion when we agree with Bill Maher, but he’s right: there is only one party where American Jews can be proudly Jewish and loudly pro-Israel, and it’s the Republican Party,” he told Fox News Digital.

“Democrats prove it again and again — from Kamala Harris passing over Josh Shapiro in 2024 to the rise of communist elected officials who traffic in antisemitism in halls of power across the country,” he continued.

“The Democratic Party is being remade by its radicalized base, and party leadership continues to fecklessly whistle past the political graveyard as American Jews flee.”

Fox News Digital reached out to the Democratic National Committee for comment but did not immediately hear back.
news.summary: "Well, in the Democratic Party, as long as that faith isn’t Jewish, you’re good," Maher retorted.
news.author: Fox News

news.title: Joe Rogan says Dems ‘full of s—‘ if they won’t specify which ‘Woke 1.0’ stances went too far
news.text:
Podcaster Joe Rogan warned Democrats the only way to escape their “woke” reputation is to give specifics on where their policies went wrong and why they were wrong to support them.

“If you really thought ‘defund the police’ and then you just ascribed it to ‘Woke 1 was crazy,’ well, how did it get you? Because it didn’t get me. How did it get you? How did ‘defund the police’ get you?” Rogan said, rhetorically asking liberals how far they actually thought about the consequences of defunding police.

“There’s a way out of it for them, but they have to be honest,” he continued. “If you want us to take you seriously, you have to say how you f—ed up,” Rogan said as he spoke about Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez’s Woke 1.0 comments. 

“You have to say how you f—ed up, and you have to say what you really think about how you f—ed up. You have to be honest, and you have to be authentic. We have to know that you are embarrassed by your choices and that you kind of went with the hive.

“If you don’t say that, then you’re full of s—. And if you’re full of s—, you’re going to get more and more full of s— over time. And that’s how politicians get soured.” 

Later in the same podcast, Rogan’s guest, YouTuber Chris Williamson, voiced skepticism that Democrats would have ever distanced themselves from Woke 1.0 in the first place if former Vice President Kamala Harris had won the election.

“Think about what would have happened if Kamala had won,” he said. “Would AOC have been talking about Woke 1.0 was crazy or would that have been a continuation of, ‘Well, look, we put the policies out, people like the policies.’ How much of this is a reversal of the position because it wasn’t effective?”

Fox News Digital reached out to Ocasio-Cortez’s office for comment. 

Commentators across the political spectrum voiced doubts about whether the modern Democratic Party actually plans to pivot from far-left cultural issues.

“I don’t believe the Democrats want to be seen backing away from wokeness, especially now that they’re sharing a ‘big tent’ from people who want to empty the prisons,” Media Research Center’s NewsBusters executive editor Tim Graham told Fox News Digital. 

“They’re just less confident than they were in 2020, when they could proclaim that race riots are ‘rebellions’ and violence was an acceptable method to create the social change they wanted. It was like political Drano.”

Democratic consultant and former House Judiciary Committee minority chief counsel Julian Epstein offered a stern warning to his party.

“There is not much difference between Woke 1 and Woke 2. They both involve the commodification of grievance and rage, and then the packaging of lunatic ideas that do little to help voters and seek to make them permanent wards of the state,” he said. 

“This is completely different from Democrats of the ’90s who would proclaim the U.S. as the best opportunity machine ever invented and then try to give people agency.”

Mary Marslender, a Republican consultant and the president and founder of Leverage PR, suggested that talk of ditching Woke 1.0 in vague terms is a cynical strategy.

“The vague talk of ditching ‘Woke 1.0’ is a temporary political strategy; it’s not genuine course correction,” she said. 

“Democrats refuse to specifically call out the craziness; they have yet to stand up for women by preventing biological males in women’s sports, stop the DEI agenda in our schools and institutions or advocate for safe communities by stopping their support of soft-on-crime progressive prosecutors. Additionally, their lack of concrete policy reversals is revealing.

“Democrats wanting to distance themselves from Woke 1 have claimed they want to ‘fix our broken immigration system,’ but such rhetoric rings hollow when they oppose interior enforcement, call to abolish ICE, defend violent illegals who have crossed our borders and unequivocally support sanctuary cities. 

“Had Harris prevailed, the same coalition that championed the 1619 Project, policing reforms adjacent to defunding and gender ideology in schools would have viewed any moderation as betrayal,” she added. 

“It’s power, not principle, that drives the Democrat Party. Until Democrats can explicitly admit fault and demonstrate a serious reversal of Woke 1, American voters are right to treat the so-called ‘post-woke’ shift as a temporary political strategy rather than a genuine course correction.”

Former Republican National Committee spokesperson Elizabeth Pipko said recent events indicate Democrats are simply responding to which way the wind blows.

“Democrats of today tend to turn with the wind,” she said. “Depending on what is most popular with their base, that’s what you’ll hear from candidates during the primaries. And then, during the presidential election, you’ll notice the Democrat nominee pretending they never supported abolishing police, men in women’s sports or abolishing [ICE].

“Watching Democrats in 2026 pretending they never called for defunding the police has been incredibly entertaining considering almost all of them still have old posts up clearly advocating for that very policy,” Pipko continued. 

“Considering how much damage some of these views have caused, it is extremely pompous to simply dismiss this time in our politics as ‘Woke 1.’ This shows how little Democrats actually believe in the what they say or do.”

Theo Wold, former White House deputy assistant for domestic policy under Trump and former assistant attorney general, suggested that even Rogan was not showing enough skepticism toward the Democrats.

“AOC’s sarcastic dismissal of Woke 1.0 isn’t a sign that Democrats are abandoning a leftist agenda. It’s a sign that they’re moving on to Ohase 2 of their project,” he said. 

“She now casually laughs at the radical ideas she actively promoted just a few years ago. And Joe Rogan, unfortunately, is too gullible to see the truth: This is who Democrats are,” Wold added. 

“They won’t abandon these ideas or apologize for them because they believe them, and when in power, they will ruthlessly advance them.”
news.summary: "If you really thought ‘defund the police’ and then you just ascribed it to ‘Woke 1 was crazy,’ well, how did it get you?" Rogan said.
news.author: Fox News

news.title: Mike Rogers' Team Asked AIPAC Not to Run Ads Against El-Sayed: Report
news.text: Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers' campaign has urged the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) not to run advertisements against Democratic rival Abdul El-Sayed, according to an Axios report on Saturday. AIPAC and its affiliated political action committees are influential players in congressional and statewide races, spending millions of dollars to support candidates, while drawing criticism from some Democrats and progressive candidates. Democratic primary voters this cycle have defied one of Washington's most influential political organizations in several primary races, delivering a series of victories to candidates running against rivals backed by AIPAC and its affiliated organizations, as was the case in Michigan’s Democratic primary. El-Sayed, a progressive Democrat who has been critical of Israel's handling of the war in Gaza, won the primary against Representative Haley Stevens earlier this month, in a race that saw around $30 million from AIPAC and affiliated groups such as United Democracy Project (UDP). Rogers, a strong supporter of Israel and who has been endorsed by President Donald Trump, will face El-Sayed in November in a closely watched race that could help determine control of the Senate. Newsweek has reached out to AIPAC and both Rogers’ and El-Sayed’s campaigns for comment via email on Saturday. What to Know Rogers' campaign urged AIPAC not to intervene in the race on his behalf, Axios reported. The outlet said Rogers spoke with AIPAC chair Michael Tuchin last week, shortly after which the organization decided not to move forward with a prepared advertisement targeting El-Sayed. The move reportedly angered AIPAC officials, who said they were prepared to spend millions more in the race to ensure El-Sayed is not elected. The decision highlights the political sensitivities surrounding AIPAC's involvement in political races, even as the group and its affiliated organizations continue to spend heavily on behalf of favored candidates. Rogers, a former congressman, has been a strong supporter of Israel, making his reported decision to push away direct AIPAC support notable. In the Michigan Democratic Senate primary, UDP had spent nearly $15 million, with roughly two-thirds of the money backing Stevens and the remainder aimed at defeating El-Sayed. Rogers’ team believes that the AIPAC-backed ads against El-Sayed backfired in the primary, per Axios. El-Sayed has described Israel’s military actions in Gaza as genocide, allegations Israel has repeatedly denied. He has also called for the end of unconditional U.S. military aid to the country. El-Sayed has criticized AIPAC's political spending and has campaigned on rejecting corporate PAC money. After his primary win, El-Sayed addressed accusations of antisemitism, saying in part, "To my Jewish American sisters and brothers ... I want you to know that my commitment to your safety, my commitment to Jewish safety, is the same commitment that I have to the safety of my own daughters." The outlet reported that talks between Rogers and AIPAC have since halted. "I welcome any and all support from the pro-Israel community and I'm proud to have their involvement," Rogers told Axios. Meanwhile, AIPAC spokesperson Deryn Sousa told the outlet: "We appreciate [former] Rep. Mike Rogers' welcoming of pro-Israel support. Our members are highly motivated to be involved in this race, and we will be looking at every option to make the case that El-Sayed's policies are bad for Michigan and bad for America." From Michigan and Minnesota Senate primaries to congressional races in New York, Illinois and California, several Democratic nominees prevailed in their races despite millions of AIPAC-affiliated spending aimed at boosting their opponents. The primary victories come amid an ongoing debate within the Democratic Party over its direction, with progressives pushing for a more left-leaning agenda while some moderates argue that such candidates could be less competitive in swing districts and statewide races. Some analysts say AIPAC's role is drawing greater scrutiny in Democratic primaries where debate over U.S. policy toward Israel has exposed divisions within the party, than it will in general elections that are often driven by a broader set of issues between Republican and Democratic candidates. Ahead of the Democratic primary, Doug Gordon, a Democratic strategist at Upshift Strategies said an El-Sayed victory would be interpreted as a setback for AIPAC. "There is no question that an El-Sayed victory would be a huge defeat for AIPAC and another sign of how toxic their brand has become within Democratic politics," Gordon told Newsweek at the time. Earlier in July, Senator Bernie Sanders, a Vermont independent who endorsed El-Sayed, described the Democratic primary as not a race "between Abdul and Haley Stevens. It is Abdul vs. AIPAC." Jim Kessler, Third Way's executive vice president for policy, previously told Newsweek that the state's demographic plays an important role in relation to AIPAC spending in the state. "It is important to remember that no state has a higher percentage of Arab-American residents in the U.S. than Michigan," Kessler said, noting that "the Jewish population is less than half that of the Arab-American population there." Michigan Political Landscape The race has drawn national attention as El-Sayed and Rogers go head-to-head to fill the open Senate seat following Democrat Gary Peters' decision to retire. Democrats have held the seat for decades, but Michigan has long defied easy political labels, often producing razor-thin elections and unexpected outcomes. Several forecasters such as The Cook Political Report and Sabato’s Crystal Ball rate the race as a "toss-up." In the 2016 presidential election, Democratic primary voters backed independent Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders over former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton. Trump later carried the state in the general election by a razor-thin margin. Since then, Michigan has alternated between Democratic and Republican presidential support, cementing its battleground status. Many of the races have been close. Trump won the state in 2024 with 49.7 percent to Vice President Kamala Harris’ 48.3 percent. In 2020, President Joe Biden won the state over Trump, 50.6 percent to 47.8 percent. Trump narrowly secured the state in his first campaign in 2016, beating Clinton by 0.23 percent, or about 10,700 votes. Democrats face a difficult map this year, needing to gain four seats while defending their own. The party has pointed to voter concerns over the economy, the ongoing Iran war and Trump’s slipping approval rating as potential opportunities to make inroads and flip the Senate. Republicans currently have a 53-47 majority in the Senate. El-Sayed vs. Rogers Polls The race has remained highly competitive in public polling, with most surveys showing Rogers and El-Sayed running within a few percentage points of each other and often any lead is within the margin of error. An AARP poll released on Thursday found El-Sayed leading Rogers by a single point, 48 percent to 47 percent. It surveyed 877 likely voters from August 9 to 11, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3.3 percentage points. It was conducted by Fabrizio Ward and Impact Research. A TechnoMetrica Institute of Policy and Politics (TIPP) survey of 1,528 registered voters in Michigan, conducted for the League of American Workers, found El-Sayed ahead with 45 percent of the vote to Rogers' 42 percent. On favorability, 39 percent of voters viewed El-Sayed favorably, while 44 percent held an unfavorable opinion and 17 percent said they had no opinion or were unsure. Rogers posted similar ratings, with 37 percent of voters viewing him favorably, 42 percent unfavorably and 21 percent saying they had no opinion or were unsure. The poll was conducted August 6-10 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 2.6 percentage points. A recent Fox News poll of 1,006 registered Michigan voters found Rogers ahead at 51 percent to 47 percent, with 2 percent undecided. The August 6-10 poll had a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points. Another recent poll, Susquehanna Polling and Research, which has been rated by Real Clear Politics as one of the most accurate pollsters, found El-Sayed leading 46 percent to 39 percent. The poll of 800 likely voters was conducted August 11-17 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.46 percentage points. Prediction markets currently give El-Sayed an edge. As of Saturday, Kalshi gave the Democrat a 61 percent chance of winning compared to 39 percent for Rogers, while Polymarket put El-Sayed's odds at 64 percent and Rogers' at 37 percent. Shifting Public Opinion on Israel The U.S. is a close ally of Israel, providing billions in military aid and diplomatic support for years. Public opinion in the U.S., however, has shifted since the aftermath of Hamas’ October 7, 2023, attack on Israel, in terms of diplomatic and military aid. Following the attack, which killed about 1,200 people and resulted in 250 hostages being taken, Israel responded with an intense military campaign in Gaza, killing over 73,000 Palestinians and triggering mass displacement. More recently, Israel and the U.S. launched coordinated strikes on Iran in late February. Recent polling shows that America has become much more divided over U.S. support for Israel, which has historically held significant support. A June AP-NORC poll found that 58 percent of Democrats said the U.S. is too supportive of Israel, up from 45 percent in January 2024, while 60 percent of Republicans said the current level of U.S. support is "about right." Overall, 31 percent of U.S. adults said they believe Israel's military actions in Gaza constitute genocide, while 49 percent said they did not know enough to say and 20 percent felt they did not constitute genocide. The survey also found Democrats have become increasingly supportive of Palestinians while support for Israel has declined within the party. Sixty-two percent said the U.S. is not supportive enough of Palestinians, up from 49 percent in January 2024. The survey of 3,040 adults was conducted from June 11 to June 17, with a margin of error of plus or minus 2.8 percentage points. A smaller subset of the AP-NORC poll looked into Jewish Americans' views. Among the bloc, polling found that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's favorability among Jewish adults is 32 percent compared to a 59 percent unfavorable rating. The poll also shows that 38 percent of respondents think the United States is too supportive of Israelis versus 24 percent who feel the U.S. is too supportive of Palestinians. When asked if they think Israel has committed genocide against Palestinians, 30 percent of Jewish adults say yes, compared to 49 percent who say no, while 21 percent say they don't know enough to answer. The study included 1,022 Jewish adults, with a 5 percent margin of error. A Pew Research survey of 12,574 Americans conducted from May 4 to May 17 found that Americans' view of the Israeli government has significantly worsened since 2022, when 65 percent of Republicans had a favorable view compared to 35 percent of Democrats. The latest survey found 51 percent of Republicans and 16 percent of Democrats feeling as such. A May Reuters/Ipsos poll found Israel's favorability rating among Democrats had fallen from 59 percent in 2018, to 22 percent. Contact Newsweek editors for this story: Steve Mollman and Anthony Murray.
news.summary: Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers asked AIPAC not to air ads targeting Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, Axios reported Saturday.

news.title: Donald Trump's wild week as BBC lawsuit descends into farce and he faces ridicule over 'close aid'
news.text: Donald Trump spent much of this week trying to avoid talking about Natalie Harp, the 'extremely close' executive assistant whose role in the White House sits somewhere between 'Oval Office gatekeeper' and 'weird security blanket'. Before we get to the rest of the week's bizarre moments, it's worth addressing why the Natalie Harp story is one that needs to be told. Some would say it's unfair to focus on a member of staff - even one employed by the most powerful and consequential man in the world. At their most innocuous, Natalie Harp's oddly close relationship with Donald Trump is the story of a young woman, perhaps a vulnerable one, whose enthusiasm and support for a political hero has turned into desperate obsession. But at worst, it illustrates the kind of messianic devotion with which Trump has surrounded himself in his second Presidency. Not all of Trump's team are so enthusiastic in their outpourings of love for their President. But Natalie Harp is not the only one who thinks he's an unquestionable gift from god. Meanwhile, Trump has been threatening to bomb the bond markets, blaming Canada, telling the Supremes not to keep him hangin' on and cosying up to Little Rocket Man. Here's everything you need to know. Donald Trump's Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent this week said he was going to double the Government's purchases of long-term US bonds in a bid to prevent a panic in the bond markets - wobbles in which have sent government borrowing costs skyrocketing. But that's not what we're looking at today. We're looking at this truly bizarre moment where Trump, asked about the intervention, appeared to have some kind of brain episode and threatened to bomb the bond market. Donald Trump has come up with a wizard new scheme for making life more expensive for regular Americans, just in time for the midterms. Blame Canada. Well, strictly speaking, each side blamed the other for trade talks breaking down on Friday night - but the upshot is both sides have slapped 50% tariffs on the other's goods. President Donald Trump’s import taxes will hit about 5% of what Canada ships to the United States every year, ranging from hockey sticks to tongue depressors. Prime Minister Carney said Ottawa would respond with targeted tariff protection for industries exposed to the new US duties, including some steel products. He also mentioned the dairy, appliance, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper and electronics sectors. No further talks were planned. Whatever the eventual outcome, a loss of trust seems one of the earliest casualties. Carney accused Washington of using “economic integration as a weapon” and said “its signature was written in pencil.” Resorting to the language of battle, he said his country had been “attacked” by the new American tariffs. “You’re at war when you get attacked,” he said, adding that Canada had the reserves, resilience and plan to respond. American ranchers used to be among Trump's fiercest defenders. And why not? He promised them a utopian future during the campaign. But he has, understandably, gone down in their estimation since it turned out he was perfectly willing to screw them in time for the midterms. In his second intervention in the beef industry this year, Trump announced he'd struck a deal to allow 300,000 metric tonnes of beef mince to be imported to the States, tariff free, over the next three months. The importers, Trump said, had agreed to sell it at 25% off market rate - in a move he said would help to "rebuild the herd" of American cattle - which is at its lowest rate for decades due to drought and high working costs for farmers. But it has the added advantage of making food a bit cheaper until shortly after America next goes to the polls. Colin Woodall, of the National Cattlemen's Beef Association, told the New York Times that "flooding the market with government-subsidized, below-market beef is not the way to rebuild the American cattle herd". And let's not forget this is the second time Trump has screwed farmers this year - after promising to import 80,000 metric tonnes of beef from Argentina in a bid to shore-up Agrie President Javier Milei's struggling government. Trump gave another one of his pre-midterms rallies in South Carolina last night. The rally was in support of Darline Graham, who is running to replace her late brother Lindsey in the Senate seat - and is rapidly proving to be a liability. But the most embarrassing thing that happened at the SC rally was the guy who stood up during Trump's speech and shouted something indecipherable, while wearing a tee shirt that read: "Kill your local paedophile." If what he was shouting was anything like as coherent as what was written on his shirt, Trump probably needn't be worried. Photos revealed by the Mirror on Friday show Donald Trump aide Natalie Harp sprinting after his cart at his Scottish golf course - confirming just one of the many bizarre tales about the President's "Human Printer." It came after bizarre letters she sent him confessing her devotion to him were published. Questions continue to be asked about the 35-year-old executive assistant's unusually close relationship with the US President. Harp is nicknamed the "human printer" because she frequently prints out and hands the President printouts of flattering news stories and cherry-picked poll numbers - acting as a "filter" for information reaching him. You can - and should - read more about the frightening letters she is said to have written to the President here. But many of the tales about Harp's behaviour are the stuff of legend, and reported, usually credited to anonymous sources, in books and longreads. Like the time she is said to have ridden in the boot of an SUV in order to stay close to Trump. So it was a pleasure to be able to confirm one of the legends - that she sprinted around Trump's Turnberry golf course on foot in 2023 - as entirely true. Pictures published by the Mirror show this incident for the first time. Harp is shown running full-tilt uphill after Trump's cart on the first day of his trip to Turnberry on 2 May 2023. Worried that she had upset Trump, Harp explained in a letter during or shortly after the trip: "The first day I was told there were no carts, and people walked, which is why I walked. "The second day, I was specifically asked by, I forget who his name was, but one of the main people who worked there, if I could continue walking, and tell any other girls who would head out there to do the same to spare the Course any more Carts. "If there is anything else I have done to cause you trouble, please forgive me." We also revealed today that Trump left his wife at home for another golf holiday in Scotland last year - on which he was accompanied by Hart. Harp accompanied Trump to Turnberry last July for a second visit - where she followed him on the golf course and sat in on at least one meeting with a world leader. You can read about that one here... Donald Trump's lawyers have badly miscalculated the President's increasingly preposterous lawsuit against the BBC in many ways. There was the original lawsuit, which would have forced Trump to hand over his financial records - we talked about that in our weekly Youtube roundup here. There was the bit where they managed to get it written down in evidence that a maximum of 285 people watched the offending Panorama programme in the United States...we talked about that in this episode - and I strongly recommend you give that one a watch if you haven't, because it's super funny. Anyway... perhaps Trump's biggest blunder was assuming the BBC was just like any other media company - and that they would fold under the threat of a 10 billion dollar lawsuit and settle out of court. See, Trump sues a lot of people - but his lawsuits seldom end up in a courtroom. Particularly when it comes to media companies, it increasingly seems that a settlement is what he's actually after. It happened with ABC News - who agreed to pay fifteen million dollars after a presenter wrongly stated that Trump had been found liable for rape, when the jury found he'd technically been found liable for sexual assault - a distinction the judge put down to a quirk of New York law. Later, Paramount settled for sixteen million dollars over an entirely spurious lawsuit relating to the editing of an interview with Kamala Harris on an episode of 60 Minutes. The interview was entirely fine, but Trump decided had been edited to present Harris in a flattering light, and Paramount had a merger they wanted to get through the regulators. So one can imagine Trump's team saw the Telegraph having a meltdown about the editing of the Panorama programme - which again, was broadly fine - and thought..."easy money." But from the beginning the Beeb has said they would fight this lawsuit to the end. And their lawyers' assertive approach to the case certainly does not give the impression they're in any mood to tell Trump "oh I suppose you're right, here's a few million quid to go away." There's just very little incentive for them to do so. They don't have a parent company that needs to do business in America. And while they are technically allowed to settle out of court, the BBC is rarely sued, and has a real appetite for defending claims it thinks are weak - not least because any payment would be taken out of licence fee cash. And suddenly the British taxpayer is effectively paying money to the leader of a foreign country over a spurious lawsuit - and it becomes a diplomatic issue. Meanwhile, Trump has been getting increasingly upset about the BBC doing entirely normal things to fight its case. See, they've issued summonses to Donald Trump Jr, Ivanka Trump and her husband Jared Kushner to give evidence in the case. The BBC says all three have personal knowledge of Trump's state of mind on January 6th. But they've been somewhat reluctant to allow themselves to be served with papers - something that usually has to be done in person in the states. And their secret service protection have declined to facilitate the process. So the beeb have gone back to the judge to ask for help in making arrangements to get these witnesses to give evidence. And that's why, on Monday, a spokesperson for Trump's legal team issued a wild statement accusing the BBC of "seeking to harass him, his family, and supporters". The beeb has now asked the court to allow service of papers to be done by email and certified mail. What makes this interesting is that in pursuing what he thought would be an easy case of extracting cash from a broadcaster, Trump may have succeeded in prompting a full-scale relitigation of what happened on January 6th - an piece of history he's spent a lot of his second presidency trying to rewrite. This could turn out to be a genuinely massive story when it lands in court next year. And if all that wasn't enough, Trump is cosying up to North Korean megadictator Kim Jong Un again. The pair have been talking again. Trump posted a picture of him and Kim taken during his first term - back when a President alienating America's natural allies while cosying up to its enemies was a novel event. Then on Sunday night he had a direct pop at South Korea, announcing he would be scaling back American involvement in a series of military drills alongside Seoul, and branding the plans "inappropriate and hostile". Trump later explained that his was partly out of revenge for South Korea refusing to help with the war on Iran. Which is not an unreasonable position for South Korea to take, given they get 60% of their oil through the Strait of Hormuz. And when he was asked about the gruesome twosome rekindling their situationship, Trump casually let slip that North Korea has "57 nukes". Which is something you don't really want to say out loud, especially in front of - as he was - the White House Press Corps and a load of contractors working on his new helipad. Supreme Court Chief Justice John Roberts is allowing the White House to continue construction on President Donald Trump’s $400 million ballroom project for now. Roberts signed a temporary order on Friday allowing work to continue while the court considers an emergency appeal from the Trump administration. Lower courts had ordered a halt to the project, finding that it must have congressional approval. Honestly, at this point the structure is like 60% built. Even if building it was illegal, what are they going to do? Order Trump to rebuild the East Wing brick by brick? Actually, yes, that would be the funniest option.
news.summary: As well as trying to avoid talking about Natalie Harp, Trump has been threatening to bomb the bond markets, blaming Canada, begging the Supremes not to keep him hangin' on and cosying up to Little Rocket Man

news.title: Bill Maher blasts Democratic Party, says it is fine with religion 'as long as that faith isn’t Jewish'

news.title: Ossoff insists he won’t run in 2028. The presidential buzz is growing anyway
news.text:
“He doesn’t want to do the job,” Ossoff said of Trump’s presidential responsibilities. “He wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie [Harp] on their apparently defenseless flying palace gifted by the emir of Qatar.”

Trump soon fired back, mocking Ossoff’s appearance and comparing the senator to the television character Pee-wee Herman.

The exchange underscored part of what has made Ossoff increasingly appealing to some Democrats online: a willingness to confront Trump directly at a moment when the party is searching for leaders capable of effectively countering the president.

“He’s gotten a lot of attention for a senator running for reelection,” Democratic strategist James Carville told the Washington Examiner. “I mean, he’s a very skilled guy. You know, he saw it as an opening, and he took it. And he’s got a very bright future in American politics, to say the least.”

The moment feeds into a phenomenon that has been building for months. Supporters are circulating clips of Ossoff’s speeches, debating his prospects against other potential 2028 Democratic contenders and increasingly comparing his trajectory with Obama’s rapid rise from the Senate to the White House.

Left-wing commentator Jeremiah Johnson recently predicted that a decisive Ossoff victory in November would send efforts to recruit him for 2028 “into turbo mode.” Sarah Longwell, a former Republican strategist, posted a photo of Ossoff in June with the caption: “President-maxxing so hard.”

Ossoff has repeatedly tried to shut down the conversation.

“I have zero interest in running for president in 2028,” Ossoff said during an appearance on MS NOW, arguing that “2028 fantasy football” risks distracting Democrats from the midterm elections.

He offered the same answer during a July 23 call with reporters when asked whether his anti-corruption message was resonating beyond Georgia.

“I’m focused on Georgia, and as I’ve said, I have zero interest in running for president in 2028,” Ossoff said.

His repeated denials have done little to quiet the speculation. Democratic strategist Michael Ceraso said the phenomenon reflects both genuine excitement around Ossoff and a recurring desire within Democratic politics to recreate an earlier political moment.

“I think it’s people’s obsession of trying to create a moment because we’re in an exhausting period of time right now,” Ceraso told the Washington Examiner.

Ceraso pointed to commentators, online creators, and former political operatives who, he said, have an “obsession with nostalgia and recreating something that feels ripe.”

“They’re definitely projecting that on Jon, for good or for bad,” he said.

Part of the attraction, Ceraso argued, is the opportunity for Democrats to project the optimism associated with Obama’s early rise onto a new candidate.

“To have like that one candidate where you can project hope and change and idealism and romanticize,” Ceraso said, comparing the early enthusiasm to the beginning of a relationship, before a candidate has been subjected to the intense scrutiny of a national campaign.

“So I’m skeptical,” he said.

At the same time, Ceraso said there is evidence Ossoff’s appeal is reaching beyond people who closely follow politics. A friend of his who does not pay much attention to politics recently came across an Ossoff speech and emailed him: “Oh my God, he’s so good.”

“I think there’s something to be said about people looking for hope,” Ceraso said. “I think that’s important.”

But he cautioned against reading too much into the reaction before the midterm elections and questioned attempts to draw a direct parallel between Ossoff and Obama, arguing that the political environments are dramatically different.

Rather than trying to recreate Obama’s moment, Ceraso said Democrats should “try to create new moments.”

Brad Bannon, another Democratic strategist, was less skeptical about where the speculation could ultimately lead.

“A senator running for reelection in 2026 is not going to announce to voters that he’s planning on turning around and running for president in 2028, but he has plenty of people who will do it for him, so it’s not a real problem,” Bannon told the Washington Examiner.

Bannon argued Ossoff could find himself particularly well positioned once the midterm elections are over because Democrats currently lack a prohibitive 2028 front-runner.

Former Vice President Kamala Harris, Gov. Gavin Newsom (D-CA), former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY) may begin with greater national name recognition, Bannon said, but none has locked down the field.

“It’s quite possible some candidate like Ossoff or like someone else can rise out of the dust and become a serious candidate,” Bannon said. “So if I was him, I’d be exploring a presidential race now, because I think the Democratic race is wide open.”

Ossoff’s reelection campaign is another reason the speculation has accelerated. The former investigative filmmaker first won his Senate seat in a 2021 runoff, narrowly defeating Republican incumbent David Perdue. Georgia then shifted back toward Republicans in 2024, when Trump carried the state by roughly 3 percentage points.

Those results initially made Ossoff’s 2026 reelection campaign appear likely to become another nail-biter. So far, it has developed differently.

Recent polling has Ossoff, 39, holding an average lead of nearly 8 percentage points over Rep. Mike Collins (R-GA), giving him a larger polling advantage than any other Senate candidate in a competitive race this cycle.

A strong victory in a battleground state could give Ossoff something many prospective 2028 contenders cannot easily claim: evidence that he can win in Trump-friendly territory. Bannon noted that Democrats have historically had success with presidential candidates from the South, pointing to former Presidents Jimmy Carter and Bill Clinton.

He also sees a more immediate geographical advantage for Ossoff: neighboring South Carolina. By Election Day, Bannon predicted, more South Carolina voters will know Ossoff because some Georgia media markets spill into the state, exposing voters to advertising from his Senate campaign.

“He’s going to have a leg up in South Carolina because, you know, he’s a neighbor,” Bannon said. “He’s the closest thing that South Carolinians have to a Democratic senator.”

The 2028 speculation is already beginning to extend beyond social media.

Ossoff has climbed sharply in prediction markets since the spring, with his chances of capturing the Democratic nomination roughly tripling and moving him into the same conversation as Newsom and Ocasio-Cortez.

Early polling is also giving supporters something to point to. An Emerson College survey testing potential 2028 contests found Ossoff ahead of both Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio in hypothetical general election matchups.

Ossoff’s approach to Israel and the war in Gaza could also become a defining part of any future national political profile. As Georgia’s first Jewish senator, Ossoff would have the potential to make history again as the country’s first Jewish president. But a presidential campaign would also test whether his identity and record on Israel become factors in a Democratic primary at a time when the war in Gaza has exposed deep divisions within the party.

In 2024, Ossoff was one of 19 senators to support Sen. Bernie Sanders’s (I-VT) initial effort to block certain U.S. arms sales to Israel, breaking with the Biden administration.

Speaking on the Senate floor at the time, Ossoff argued Washington needed to use its leverage over its ally as the civilian toll mounted in Gaza. The vote initially appeared politically risky for a Democrat who would eventually face reelection in a battleground state. But Democrats have since moved substantially closer to Ossoff’s position, giving supporters another point of comparison with Obama, whose early opposition to the Iraq War preceded a broader shift within his party.

The prospect of a Jewish nominee also raises a broader question for Democrats as they look toward 2028: whether the party is ready to nominate its first Jewish presidential candidate amid an increasingly contentious debate over Israel.

Democratic strategists interviewed by the Washington Examiner largely dismissed the idea that Ossoff’s Jewish identity itself would present an obstacle.

“I think if we stop acknowledging these questions, like primary candidates, stop worrying about answering that question and just run for office, we’ll be in a lot better place,” Ceraso said.

Ceraso, who has worked for candidates from a variety of backgrounds, compared the question to those he encountered while working for Buttigieg’s presidential campaign about whether voters were ready to support a gay candidate.

“Just think about what you want from your candidate and whether that candidate, if they’re in office, would be the best leader possible,” Ceraso said, arguing Democrats should “let people run and let the voters decide.”

Bannon was similarly unequivocal when asked whether Democrats were prepared to nominate a Jewish candidate.

“The short answer is yes,” Bannon said, pointing out that Gov. Josh Shapiro (D-PA), who is also Jewish, is already considered another prominent potential Democratic presidential contender.

“It’s going to be an issue in the campaign,” Bannon added, before reiterating: “I think Democrats are ready.”

For now, Ossoff has a more immediate test in Georgia. But if he emerges from November with a decisive victory in one of the country’s premier battleground states, the online effort to imagine him as a presidential candidate is unlikely to disappear.

And Bannon suspects Ossoff may eventually have reason to listen.

“My basic feeling about the race is completely wide open now,” Bannon said. “If you have Potomac fever, you want to live in the White House. This is the time to run.”
news.summary: Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-GA) insists he has “zero interest” in running for president in 2028, but a growing corner of the Democratic internet is acting as though he may not get the final say. The Georgia Democrat’s national profile has surged in recent weeks as clips of his increasingly combative attacks on President Donald Trump […]

news.title: ELDER- Obama to tell the brothers to vote for El-Sayed  The North State Journal
news.text:
Former President Barack Obama will likely campaign for Abdul El-Sayed, the far-left Democrat who just won Michigan’s U.S. Senate primary.

The two spoke after the primary, and El-Sayed publicly said he hopes Obama will campaign for him. Michigan could determine control of the Senate, and Obama remains the most popular Democrat.

El-Sayed won despite performing poorly among black primary voters. His coalition skewed younger, whiter, college-educated and progressive. In Detroit, Michigan’s largest majority-black city, El-Sayed’s opponent won more than 60% of the Democratic Senate vote. That may work in a Democratic primary. But will it work in November?

Enter Obama.

During the 2024 presidential campaign, Obama visited a Kamala Harris campaign office in Pittsburgh and said he wanted to “speak some truths.” He complained that enthusiasm for Harris was weaker than when he ran and said the problem “seems to be more pronounced with the brothers.”

 “You’re coming up with all kinds of reasons and excuses. I’ve got a problem with that,” Obama said, suggesting some black men “just aren’t feeling the idea of having a woman as president.”

Apparently, some of “the brothers” remained unpersuaded. Pew Research Center’s validated-voter analysis later estimated that 21% of black men voted for Donald Trump. Nevertheless, Obama will probably go to Michigan and explain to black voters who rejected El-Sayed in the primary why they should vote for him in November. After all, Obama and El-Sayed are closely aligned on policy.

Take healthcare. El-Sayed supports Medicare for All. Obama repeatedly said the ideal healthcare plan would be single-payer. “If I were starting a system from scratch,” Obama said in 2009, “then I think that the idea of moving towards a single-payer system could very well make sense.” Near the end of his second term, Obama said, “If I was starting from scratch, I probably would have supported a single-payer system.”

Then-Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid (D-Nev.) called it a goal. Asked in 2013 whether Obamacare was ultimately a step toward single-payer healthcare, Reid answered, “Yes, yes. Absolutely, yes.”

Like Obama, El-Sayed chastises “the rich” for “not paying their fair share in taxes.” Like Obama, who said racism is part of America’s “DNA,” El-Sayed believes racism remains a serious problem.
