news.title: Trump’s coalition fractures as midterm reckoning looms
news.text: Donald Trump’s name will not appear on the ballot when Americans vote on November 3, but the midterm elections are increasingly shaping up as a referendum on his presidency. Less than two years after returning to the White House with a victory that dramatically expanded the Republican coalition, Trump now faces sharp erosion among independent voters, Hispanics and more moderate Republicans, even as his core MAGA base remains overwhelmingly loyal. The stakes are enormous. Republicans currently hold narrow control of the House and a Senate majority. Losing either chamber would make it significantly harder for Trump to advance legislation, confirm nominees and avoid congressional investigations during the final two years of his term. The central problem for Republicans is that Trump’s 2024 coalition extended well beyond traditional MAGA voters. He made major gains among Hispanics, younger voters and working-class Americans, while also attracting people who did not consider themselves reliable Republicans. Pew analysis found that 48% of Hispanic voters backed Trump in 2024, up from 36% in 2020, with especially strong gains among Hispanic men and voters without college degrees. Now, parts of that coalition are moving away. The reasons vary. For many Hispanic voters, the economy is central. Among independents, frustration reflects a combination of the cost of living, the war in Iran and broader dissatisfaction with the president. Inside the Republican Party, the divide between loyal MAGA supporters and more moderate Republicans is becoming increasingly visible. For congressional candidates, however, the reason matters less than the result: some of the voters who helped Trump win in 2024 are no longer in the same place politically. The nearly six-month war with Iran has added another major burden for Trump. He returned to office promising to tackle the cost of living and avoid prolonged wars. Instead, the conflict has disrupted oil trade through the Strait of Hormuz and contributed to higher fuel prices, turning a foreign-policy crisis into an immediate economic issue for American households. A Reuters/Ipsos poll published this week put Trump’s approval rating at 33%, the lowest of his current term, while 64% said they disapproved of his performance. Eight in 10 Americans believe U.S. involvement in Iran will continue for a long time, including 71% of Republicans. Only one in five Americans said the war had been worth the cost. An Economist/YouGov poll painted a similarly difficult picture. Fifty-seven percent said going to war was the wrong decision, while only 25% said it was the right one. Sixty-five percent want Washington to reach an agreement ending the conflict as quickly as possible, including 48% of Republicans. Among independent voters, 61% believe the war will last at least another year. For many voters, the debate over Iran ultimately comes down to what they pay at the gas station. Why the midterms matter Midterm elections are held halfway through a president’s four-year term. The presidency is not on the ballot, but all 435 seats in the House of Representatives are. Republicans currently hold a narrow House majority, meaning even a relatively small shift in competitive districts could hand control to Democrats. If Democrats capture the House, they could block or delay White House legislation, control congressional committees, launch investigations and summon administration officials for testimony. The Senate operates differently. Senators serve six-year terms, with roughly one-third of seats contested every two years. In November, 33 regularly scheduled seats will be up for election, along with additional special elections. Republicans currently hold 53 Senate seats, while Democrats have 45. Two independents, Bernie Sanders and Angus King, caucus with Democrats, effectively giving the Democratic bloc 47 votes. That means Democrats would need four more seats to reach 51 and control the Senate outright. Losing the Senate would also make it harder for Trump to secure confirmation of senior administration officials and judges. MAGA remains loyal. The problem is everyone else Trump’s core support remains exceptionally strong. In an Economist/YouGov poll conducted August 14-17, 95% of Republicans who identified as MAGA supporters approved of his performance, while only 4% disapproved. But among Republicans who do not identify with MAGA, approval dropped to 59%, with 40% disapproving. That divide is increasingly visible even on immigration, one of Trump’s signature issues. A new POLITICO poll found that 50% of Americans believe the administration’s mass deportation campaign has become too aggressive. Nearly a quarter of voters who backed Trump in 2024 also said the policy had gone too far. Reuters/Ipsos data show another warning sign: the Republican advantage over Democrats on which party is better equipped to handle immigration has collapsed from 26 percentage points at the start of 2025 to just two points today. Trump is not facing a revolt from his base. The danger is that the voters around that base are weakening in their support. No group better illustrates that shift than Hispanic men. They were among Trump’s biggest electoral success stories in 2024, helping Republicans argue that the old assumption that minority voters would reliably support Democrats was beginning to break down. CNN polling analyst Harry Enten presented data this week showing how dramatically that support has changed. Trump won Hispanic men by 10 percentage points in 2024. His current net approval among them stands at minus 41, a 51-point swing. On the economy, the shift is even larger. Before the 2024 election, Hispanic men preferred Trump over Kamala Harris on economic issues by 11 points. His current net rating on the economy among that group is minus 49, a 60-point reversal. The comparison is not exact, since election results and approval ratings measure different things. But CNN also presented data directly tied to the coming congressional vote. Republicans won Hispanic men by eight points in the 2024 congressional elections. Democrats now lead among them by 20 points, a 28-point shift. Independents move sharply away Independent voters may be even more important. According to Ipsos data cited by CNN, Trump’s net approval among independents now stands at minus 47. At the beginning of his second term, it was minus one. Economist/YouGov found that only 21% of independents approve of his performance, while 74% disapprove. That does not mean all of those voters will support Democrats. Some may vote for local Republican candidates, choose independents or simply stay home. And that may be enough to hurt the GOP. In close congressional districts, Republicans do not necessarily need Trump voters to defect to Democrats. They simply need too many of them to lose motivation and stay home. Inside the party, signs of unease are already visible. Republican Sen. Jim Justice of West Virginia said this week that anyone failing to see how Americans are being hurt by food and fuel prices is “living in a cave,” arguing that Republicans need to pay more attention to economic pressure on voters. Arizona Republican strategist Barrett Marson put the political danger even more starkly, telling CNN that there is one person who is not sufficiently worried about gas prices, and that “one person controls our fate”: Trump. Congress has also seen defections over the Iran war. In July, four House Republicans joined Democrats in supporting a resolution calling for an end to U.S. military operations against Iran without congressional authorization. The measure was largely symbolic, but it highlighted the extent to which the war has become a political problem even within the GOP. ‘Why should we vote if he isn’t doing what he promised?’ Behind the polling are voters who supported Trump in 2024 and are now reconsidering their political choices. Reuters has been following a group of Trump voters throughout his second term. The group is not statistically representative, but their interviews offer a glimpse into the mood among parts of the coalition that returned him to office. Juan Rivera, 26, from the San Diego area, said he still intends to vote for Republican candidates. But while canvassing Latino voters, he encountered disappointed Trump supporters who had lost enthusiasm. “Why should I vote when the president isn’t doing what he promised?” he said some voters asked him. Steve Egan, a 65-year-old Florida business owner who voted for Trump, told Reuters that tariffs had increased his business costs while the war had pushed up fuel and other prices. His opinion of Trump had deteriorated so much, he said, that an endorsement from the president could now make him less likely to support a candidate. Robert Billups of Washington state said he no longer feels committed to Republican candidates and will vote in November for whoever offers what he considers the best plan, regardless of party. These voters are not necessarily becoming Democrats. That is precisely the problem. The coalition beyond MAGA Trump still dominates the Republican Party, and loyalty among MAGA voters remains extraordinarily high. But he did not win in 2024 only because of voters who would support him under almost any circumstances. He won by expanding the coalition, drawing in Hispanic men, working-class voters, independents and people who had not previously been reliable Republican voters. In November, Republicans need those voters again, but Trump himself will not be on the ballot to draw them out. Democrats currently lead registered voters 46% to 39% in the Economist/YouGov generic congressional ballot. Among voters who say they are extremely enthusiastic about voting, the gap is much wider: 60% say they plan to vote Democratic, compared with 37% Republican. Trump’s MAGA base remains intact. The question facing Republicans is whether the broader coalition that returned him to power still exists. For now, the numbers suggest it is beginning to fracture.
news.summary: Approval falls to 33% as independents, Hispanics and moderate Republicans drift away, while the Iran war and cost of living threaten GOP control of Congress

news.title: Biden-Era Law That Created Medicare Drug Price Controls Could Hike Up Prices, Analysts Warn
news.text:
Medicare’s drug price controls could restrict Americans’ ability to access care and potentially drive up costs in the long term, according to analysts.

The Inflation Reduction Act (IRA), signed into law by then-President Joe Biden in August 2022, authorized the U.S. federal government to negotiate prices for certain high-cost prescription drugs covered by Medicare through the Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program. While congressional Democrats previously claimed the IRA would help bring down healthcare prices, analysts warned the Daily Caller News Foundation that such price controls might limit some patients’ access to certain prescription medicines and impose cost burdens on Americans. (RELATED: What Is Causing US Prescription Drug Costs To Plummet?)

“Despite the IRA’s drug price controls being sold as a boon to consumers, the policy doesn’t actually solve any of the health-policy problems people consider most important to them,” Director of Health Policy at Americans for Tax Reform Isabelle Marchese told the DCNF. “Price controls don’t eliminate cost or risk; they simply reallocate them in less efficient, less transparent ways. To protect their income, insurers and PBMs have, naturally, responded by tightening their utilization-management tools — prior authorization, quantity limits, formulary exclusions, and/or preferred-status restrictions — on the drugs whose list or net prices have been artificially suppressed.”

“These results are inevitable consequences of price controls,” Marchese continued. “They never make the underlying costs or risks disappear, they only force someone else (often, patients) to absorb them through more red tape, delayed care, and restricted access.”

Traditionally, a price control refers to a mandate that requires a business to reduce the price of its product to what the government deems an acceptable level, according to Americans for Prosperity. Throughout history, socialist countries have often imposed such controls.

Marchese went on to say that such price controls may further reduce patient access to select prescription drugs in the future.

“Not only will these price controls cause drug price hikes and limit access in the near future, but the long-term effects of this policy are even more devastating,” she said. “In the near term, companies will raise launch prices on new drugs, accelerate price increases on non-selected products, and shift costs onto the commercial market that covers the majority of Americans under 65. In the long term, many of the high-risk, high-reward research projects that made the U.S. the world leader in biomedical innovation will never be started.”

The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) released its first proposed rule in June to solidify regulations governing the IRA’s Drug Price Negotiation Program for Initial Price Applicability Year (IPAY) 2029 and future years, according to Hogan Lovells Cadwalader.

After the coverage requirement for IPAY 2026-selected drugs went into effect during the first quarter of the year, 24% of first fill attempts for these drugs were initially rejected, which indicates “a lack of material improvement for patient access,” according to a recent analysis from IQVIA. This rejection rate was unchanged from 2025, per the report.

CMS plans to issue the final rule to implement the Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program for initial price applicability year 2029 and years thereafter in fall 2026, according to a fact sheet. The agency also intends to issue final revised information collection requests on the data and information the Federal government will collect to inform drug selection and drug price negotiation and submit the collection to the Office of Management and Budget for final approval, per the fact sheet.

Trump has previously criticized price controls and highlighted their longtime association with leftist regimes. In August 2024, Trump blasted then-Vice President Kamala Harris’ proposal for a food price-gouging ban as “communist” price controls, NBC News reported.

Despite this, some experts have previously compared Trump’s May 2025 executive order aiming to broaden Americans’ “access to the most-favored-nation price” for prescription drugs to imposing such controls.

”CMS is focused on delivering lower prescription drug costs for seniors while protecting taxpayers and preserving access to innovative treatments,” A CMS spokesperson told the DCNF. “Although the Medicare prescription drug market continues to adapt to significant changes enacted by Congress, CMS is closely examining emerging cost trends and using every available tool to promote affordability, competition, transparency, and responsible stewardship of taxpayer dollars.”

“This includes doubling the amount of estimated savings in the second year of the Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program,” the spokesperson added. “The Administration is committed to building a Medicare drug program that puts American patients first, securing better value, strengthening accountability across the system, and ensuring seniors have access to the medicines they need at prices they can afford.”

The White House did not respond to the DCNF’s request for comment.

A No Patient Left Behind (NPLB) survey published in March found that 92% of beneficiaries expect they will face higher out-of-pocket costs under the IRA. Meanwhile, 30% of beneficiaries said their Medicare Part D plan initially denied them access to a drug prescribed by their doctor, NPLB’s research shows.

This week’s #ParagonPic, adapted from recent @Health_Affairs analysis, highlights:Private plans were successfully negotiating #drugprices without price controls. 💊Read more from @theomerkel for @SenateFinance ⬇️https://t.co/8hNGTlSj2n pic.twitter.com/6Cxv2rPAuE— Paragon Health Institute (@Paragon_Inst) September 18, 2024

The IRA “is not delivering the outcomes that Democrats promised,” according to Pacific Research Institute President and CEO Sally Pipes.

“The IRA was sold as a way to make medicines more affordable and accessible, yet nearly one in four patients trying to start one of the first 10 price-controlled drugs was initially denied,” Pipes told the DCNF. “For some of the sickest patients, the rejection rates were much higher. Initial rejection rates reached 67% for the selected oncology medicines and 59% for the immunology medicines, according to IQVIA data. Even a month after the initial attempt, 16% of oncology claims and 22% of immunology claims remained rejected.”

This “underscores the reality that government price controls have a negative impact on improving patients’ access to medicines,” Pipes added.

Still, a KFF poll released in September 2024 found that 85% of voters backed letting the federal government negotiate prices for some prescription drugs for people enrolled in Medicare.

Republican North Carolina Rep. Greg Murphy claimed in a July 8 X post that Americans’ “access to care and critical drugs will be crushed” by the IRA’s Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program.

Access to care and critical drugs will be crushed by the Inflation Reduction Act’s (IRA) Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program.Proud to work in a bipartisan effort to reverse the short-sighted reimbursement formula and protect patient healthcare.https://t.co/17T4U4kbe8— Congressman Greg Murphy, M.D. (@RepGregMurphy) July 8, 2026

Pipes also told the DCNF that the IRA may be “deterring companies from investing in medical research and development” across the nation.

“I would not be surprised if these denial rates and utilization management continue to rise, as IRA price controls apply to a larger and larger number of medicines each year,” she explained. “But arguably more important, the law is deterring companies from investing in medical research and development, which will have severe long-term consequences for Americans’ physical and financial health.”

news.title: 'It’s chaos': Trump rewards red state farmers with blown profits this year
news.text:
MS NOW reporter Alex Tabet says there’s a very obvious reason the state of Iowa is slipping out of Republicans’ grasp this midterm, and it has everything to do with the Trump economy.

“It's chaos,” said Iowa Farmers Association President Aaron Lehman, speaking with Tabet on a Saturday morning show. “You know, we are just not on the right path at the time. When farmers are dealing with all this uncertainty, we should be doing more to help them bring stability.”

“We should be passing a farm bill that's three years overdue to provide some stability for farmers. No passage in sight yet. We should be doing more to have a trade policy that gets to fair prices for farmers with fair practices for farmers. We're not getting any closer to that,” Lehman added. “It's just chaos. So, the chaotic situation makes it so hard for farmers to plan on how they can put a crop in the ground, harvest it and expect a reasonable return.”

Tabet, reporting from Lehman’s fifth generation corn, soybean and hay farm, said life on the farm is more expensive than ever.

“This farm operates three tractors … and about a year ago, it was $3.50 per gallon for diesel. Now it's $5.40. Each of these things guzzle about 100 gallons a day. So some quick math will show you for each tractor during harvest season, that's an additional $200 per tractor, $600 in total,” said Tabet.

But that is just one of the many factors that farmers are having to contend with, he added. Equipment and machinery purchase and repairs are significantly more expensive under Trump’s tariffs, and the food they grow, including corn and soybeans are contenting with retaliative tariffs from other countries due to Trump’s tariffs.

“Not to mention the fact that every single farm in America has to purchase fertilizer, and fertilizer costs are up 12 percent in the first quarter of 2026 because of this war in Iran, because of the strait of Hormuz,” said Tabet.

When asking Lehman and other farmers at the Iowa State Fair if their farm was profitable last year, the most common answer was ‘No.” The answer remained a solid “no” when asked if they expected to break even this season, as well.

Lehman, as president of the organization did not say who he voted for in the last election, but the state of Iowa — and farmers in particular — were deep in the fold for President Trump in the last election.

“What I can tell you is we are here in Iowa President Trump won 98 of the 99 counties in the caucuses. He won the state, beating Kamala Harris by 14 points in 2024,” said Tabet. “This is Trump country. But at the same time, the Cook Political Report just put the gubernatorial race as “lean Democratic” for [candidate] Rob Sand and a “toss up” for [Senate candidate] Josh Turek. These are races that shouldn't be this close. But because of these economic conditions, at least according to the Cook Political Report, they are.”

news.title: This rare Nebraska district backed Harris but sent a Republican to Congress. Can Democrats win here?
news.text:
OMAHA, Neb. (AP) — “Do they still like Trump in Nebraska? I think so,” the president said during a recent event in Washington.

Given that the state easily backed Republican Donald Trump three times and hasn’t supported a Democrat for the White House since Lyndon B. Johnson in 1964, the answer may seem obvious.

But in Nebraska’s largest city, it’s an open question and could decide one of the country’s most-watched congressional races. Retiring Rep. Don Bacon ’s open seat pits fellow Republican and Omaha City Councilmember Brinker Harding against Democratic activist Denise Powell.

The district encompasses an increasingly Democratic-leaning Omaha metro area of 1 million-plus and its more conservative suburbs — famous for steaks and the Reuben sandwich’s birthplace, though New York disputes that.

It’s one of just eight districts nationwide that elected Republicans in House races while supporting Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris over Trump two years ago.

Harding and Powell have been making the rounds at parades and festivals where meat raffles offer oversized sausages as prizes. However, those on-the-ground appeals could be drowned out by Trump who, like most things in politics, has moved to shape November’s midterm elections in his own image.

The president is organizing a Republican midterm convention in Dallas next month that will serve as much a two-day rally for him as a boon to party candidates nationwide. Trump is also frequently visiting tightly contested districts, despite his low approval ratings and the unpopular war in Iran.

While Trump centers himself, Democrats are happy to oblige.

When Powell knocks on doors to talk to voters, she asks, “What’s keeping you up at night?” On a sweaty Saturday afternoon, John Rosseter responded without hesitation. “Well, Trump.”

“I want to see the history books written years from now,” said Rosseter, 67, who owns a carpentry business. “They won’t be pretty.”

The ‘Blue Dot’ hasn’t helped Democratic House candidates

Nebraska splits its presidential electoral votes, and the 2nd Congressional District’s delegate has gone to Democrats three out of five times since 2008, making it a “ blue dot ” in an otherwise Republican red state. But a Democrat has won the House seat just once since 1994.

Harding plays up Trump’s primary endorsement, and House Speaker Mike Johnson and Majority Leader Steve Scalise campaigned for him. Harding said he has “the full confidence of, not only the White House, but leadership in the Congress.”

He has also tried to appeal to swing voters and says he knows the district better than does Powell, co-founder of Women Who Run Nebraska, which supports female candidates.

Two possible Democratic 2028 presidential candidates — ex-Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg and Rahm Emanuel, an ex-Chicago mayor who was President Barack Obama’s first White House chief of staff — have campaigned with Powell.

She talks about how Medicare cuts have increased anxiety about affordability. Powell also points to Trump and his family’s business dealings as an example of “the choices that they have made while people on the ground are struggling” and she says that resonates with Republicans.

“Even the ones who aren’t necessarily anti-Trump,” Powell said, “understand the need for checks and balances.”

Some Democrats want a ‘Blue Dot Wave’

Jason Brown and his wife, Ruth Huebner-Brown, caused a sensation in 2024 by spray painting about 50 reused lawn signs with blue dots and distributing them around Omaha’s Dundee neighborhood. The couple has since expanded to professionally produce signs promoting a “Blue Dot Wave.”

Brown said the Republican-controlled Congress has capitulated on “every Trump nominee, every Trump policy, all the way down to putting gilding gold on statues.”

Supporters of Harding have countered with red “Brinker Dot” signs.

“We need to make sure that we keep this country on the track to being even better,” Harding said.

Jack Hosking, the 90-year-old retired former head of a title insurance company, organizes a weekly coffee to discuss political and community issues. He estimated that about 70% of attendees are Trump voters and “maybe even more so lately, because of the crap that the New York mayor started,” referring to Zohran Mamdani’s efforts at pushing the Democratic Party to the left.

Both Powell and Harding have addressed Hosking’s group, though, and he predicted that as much as half will support the Democrat.

“She spoke well enough that, my sense is, a lot of them will cross over,” Hosking said, noting that when it came to campaigning, “Brinker’s not doing much.”

The president seen as a base motivator

The Republican National Committee views Trump as a national asset, betting he can prevent complacency in a year without a presidential race, when enthusiasm for the party in power typically wanes.

The committee rebranded its “Young Guns” program for key candidates to “MAGA Majority” in deference to Trump’s “Make America Great Again” movement, and many congressional candidates will be at the Dallas convention with Trump.

Others aren’t waiting that long.

Republican Reps. Mike Lawler of New York and Tom Barrett of Michigan, whom Democrats are aiming to unseat, both appeared with Trump during his rallies in their districts. When the president visited Macungie, Pennsylvania, in June, he joined Republican Rep. Ryan Mackenzie, saying, “I’m here for him.”

Trump also traveled to the Wisconsin district of Republican Rep. Derreck Van Orden, as have Cabinet members.

Rep. Juan Ciscomani, facing a reelection fight, appeared with Trump during an April event in Arizona. Two Iowa Republicans in what could be toss-up reelection contests, Reps Zach Nunn and Mariannette Miller-Meeks, both were by Trump’s side when he kicked off his midterm campaign outside Des Moines.

Bacon sometimes defied the White House in his final term. He criticized Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and tried to curb Trump’s ability to impose tariffs and was the only House Republican who opposed renaming the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America.

Mary Jane Truemper, who heads the Nebraska Republican Party, said Powell and the state’s Democrats have moved too far to the left. She called Harding “a steady force” and said the nominee is not as fond of picking high-profile fights the way Bacon sometimes was.

“I think he speaks to the moderate Democrats as well as the Republicans,” said Truemper, who managed Bacon’s reelection campaign in 2018 and also worked for an unsuccessful primary challenger to him.

Even Powell said, “Don Bacon was a good representative of this district, and I think that there are a lot of people drawn to a pragmatic style of leadership in a state like ours.” But that may not be enough this year.

“People are worse off than they were before,” Powell said.

A local race may expose a wider party divide among neighbors

In the Elmwood Park neighborhood, Andy Maxwell, a 58-year-old pediatrician, said he likes to find the middle ground in politics and his community. But he recalled that, after putting up a Biden sign in his yard in 2020, his neighbors erected a Trump one.

“We don’t like all the turmoil part of it,” Maxwell said of politics nationally.

Nearby, 80-year-old Jerard Pearson called Democrats “feckless,” but said of Trump’s base supporters, “I’ve always been curious about this one-third level of crazy out there, a third of the population.” He is also no fan of a neighbor’s large “Harding for Congress” sign.

Truemper said Harding appreciates Trump’s endorsement but Nebraskans like to be wooed “person-to-person, rather than a national entity coming in.”

“Is that going to be the deciding factor?” she asked of Trump. “I don’t know.”

news.title: National groups ramp up spending in rural AZ congressional district
news.text:
It would be tough for Democrats to flip one of Arizona's rural, conservative-leaning congressional districts this year, but that hasn't stopped national political groups from pouring in money.

Both parties are funneling resources into the seat held by incumbent Republican Rep. Eli Crane as polling suggests Republicans could face serious headwinds in this year's midterms.

Crane won reelection in Arizona's 2nd Congressional District by nearly 10 points in 2024, roughly 55%-45%.

He is now locked in a rematch against the same Democratic candidate, former Navajo Nation President Jonathan Nez.

The district, which includes a large swath of northeastern Arizona, favors Republicans and historically has voted for President Donald Trump by double-digit margins. But the uptick in spending is a sign both parties are keeping tabs on the district during a midterm cycle that could be challenging for the GOP.

"I would still categorize it as a reach opportunity," said Erin Covey, an analyst with the non-partisan Cook Political Report. "Democrats do have a credible path to victory, even if it is narrow."

Race heats up, at least on paper

The race appears to be heating up, at least on paper.

Crane and Nez have ramped up their fundraising since the last election cycle.

The size of Crane's campaign war chest has roughly doubled since 2024, records show. He has received more than $800,000 from House Republican leaders, a steep increase from years past. Nez, too, is bringing in more cash, raising about four times as much money compared to 2024.

But Crane's campaign still had the edge heading into August. He had raised about twice as much as Nez in total and spent four times as much.

Outside groups have been mobilizing in the district. Several Democratic-aligned groups have spent more than $750,000 in an ongoing attack ad campaign targeting the congressman, a sizable spend with more than two months to go before the election.

Non-partisan political analysts still rate the race as "likely" safe for Republicans.

Covey said the spending patterns mirror what's happening in other races where Republicans have a modest advantage. It makes sense for Democrats to start spending money, she said, but it might be more of a trial balloon to see how effective their attacks are, and whether it's worth investing even more money into the district as November approaches.

Arizona district becoming a priority

Democrats have emphasized that Nez performed several points better than their party's presidential candidate Kamala Harris in the district during the 2024 cycle, raising liberal hopes of an upset victory. Even if Nez repeats that strong performance, he still has a lot of ground to make up. The district strongly favored Trump during the 2020 and 2024 presidential cycles, illustrating its Republican tilt.

Liberal spenders hope this campaign cycle will bring new opportunities.

The recent attack ads, a joint effort by the League of Conservation Voters and a Latino voter engagement group, have highlighted Crane's opposition to clean energy tax credits in an attempt to win over voters who are concerned about their energy bills.

Nez's campaign has elevated pocketbook issues.

"Regardless of the money Crane and his billionaire friends will pour in this election season to deceive Arizona voters, Nez is focused on a campaign built on protecting our water, lowering costs, improving infrastructure, and taking our government back from the hands of the elites," Mark Hatton, a campaign spokesperson, wrote in a statement to The Republic.

Crane, for his part, has leaned into some rural Arizonans' skepticism of clean-energy projects, railing against "green new deal" policymaking and describing large wind and solar farms as being driven by "corporate elites." He's also promoted the Republican-led tax cut package he helped pass last year.

"Selling out rural Arizonans to avoid a third straight electoral loss is a bold strategy by Mr. Nez," wrote Greg Smith, a Crane spokesperson.

His district isn't at the top of the GOP's list of priorities. About two dozen seats, including two in Arizona, are generally regarded as much more competitive and have seen significantly more spending by both political parties.

The clearest sign of the district's competitiveness will be if national Republican Party groups mobilize to defend Crane, said Covey, like they're doing in the top battleground seats. But that hasn't happened yet.

"If they actually come and insert spending here, then we'll know he is truly vulnerable," she said.

news.title: Is Trump dragging Republicans down?
news.text:
It’s the Democrats who have mostly had to answer questions about electability this midterm season, but why are there so few questions about the “E” word for the other side?
Gas prices are still skyrocketing. A number of Republican candidates, such as Ohio Rep. Max Miller and former Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, who’s running for a Senate seat, are mired in scandal. The Iran war was unpopular from the start, but it is getting even less popular as it drags on. And Trump’s approval rating recently hit 33 percent, the lowest of his presidency yet.
On this week’s episode of America, Actually, host Astead Herndon speaks with one of Trump’s most vocal defenders, conservative influencer CJ Pearson, about whether we’re seeing Trump’s brand slip even among his supporters and the young people who helped him win in 2024, and how that could affect the midterm elections. 
Pearson, a conservative content creator and influencer, first went viral when he posted himself, then 12 years old, criticizing Barack Obama in a YouTube video. Now 24, Pearson is one of MAGA’s most prominent Black voices.
In this episode, Astead and Pearson discussed how Republicans should answer questions about whether voters’ lives are better than they were two years ago; whether Trump still has any cultural cachet left over from his last presidential campaign; and when Pearson started to see young Republicans turning away from the MAGA movement.
Below is an excerpt of Astead’s conversation with Pearson, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full show, so listen to America, Actually wherever you get your podcasts or watch it on Vox’s YouTube channel.
[Media: https://open.spotify.com/show/0xv3qPaQ9tu0l5zyz7AQkx?si=2d127db4ff3644af]
That “E” word’s been thrown around a lot about Democrats, but we want to think about how Republicans are on their own. If you could rate Donald Trump’s second term one through 10, what would you give it?
I think the president’s doing incredibly well for the American people. Promises made, promises kept in many ways. 
I think if you look at this president who ran on securing our southern border, he’s done it. You look at this president who’s talked about bringing down costs, he’s brought down the cost of dairy, eggs. He’s achieved that. 
And I think also this president is only just getting started. He ran on “no tax on tips.” He did that. He ran on “no tax on overtime.” He did that. Oftentimes I tell people the challenge of this administration is keeping up the messaging at the same pace as the accomplishments of this president.
And so I think that there’s a lot more work to do. Thankfully, we have two more years to do it.
Can I get a number?
I think he’s doing well. I will say I grew up in a place where there’s always room for improvement, so I’ll give him an eight.
You’re giving him an eight. I wanted to just start there because Trump’s approval rating has fallen, as I’m sure you have seen. Why do you think the country isn’t maybe on the same page as you?
I think a lot of people are focused on their pocketbooks, right? They’re focused on domestic issues, and I think that we have been very internationally focused over the course of the past few months as we’ve navigated and dealt with the Iran conflict. 
But I think that as we get ready to get through this last wave of primaries, I think you’re going to see a change in his messaging and a reset at the midterm convention in Dallas next month in September. 
And I think you’re going to hear this president talking about how he’s made America more affordable, how he’s kept Americans safe, far safer than they were under President Joe Biden.
And I think that you’ll see those numbers start to change. And a reminder, the only poll that matters is on Election Day. There are many polls that had Kamala Harris beating President Trump, in 2024, and that didn’t happen.
Yeah, I don’t want to be overly poll-reliant, but we’ve heard some of this directly from Republicans even. 
We were at Donald Trump’s UFC event in DC talking to young men, and even there we heard people really come to be critical on three issues specifically: tariffs, the Iran war, and the handling of the Epstein files.
You mentioned the question of affordability. Donald Trump has said, quote, “I love the inflation.” And when asked by reporters about the public strain that has come from the conflicts with Iran, he said, “I don’t think about Americans’ financial situation. I don’t think about anybody.”
How can you say that Republicans are gonna run on affordability if the president’s saying he doesn’t care if Americans’ lives are unaffordable?
Well, I’ve often said that we can’t cede this entire affordability debate to the Democrats. The reason that I think a lot of young people are giving a little bit, even a flirtatious nod to the DSA and their socialist and communist candidates, is because they’re talking about an issue that’s top of mind for them.
In the same way that when President Trump won in 2024, he was talking about issues that were top of mind of the American voter, which was the cost of living. 
And so I think that we need to get back to that messaging. I think that this president has continued to deliver on that front. Costs are coming down.
The economy is resurging. We’re seeing economic and global investment in this country unlike anything we’ve seen before. In Oklahoma, we’re bringing back manufacturing with the aluminum smelting plant.
But the president’s not saying this. The president’s saying, “I love the inflation, and I don’t think about Americans’ financial situation.” Do those words help Republican midterm candidates?
Well, I think the president has a lot of time to say a lot more things because Election Day is pretty far away from now. I think we have two or three months left, and I think the president will make this case. 
But I think what will also make the case is that the candidates that the Democrats are running and nominating all across this country, who are now affiliating themselves with the socialist movement, are not actually fighting for things that will actually ever work.
Socialism has never worked anywhere it’s been tried, and I think that this is going to be an election between common sense versus crazy. Do you wanna run a candidate that hates Thanksgiving?
For the record, that candidate lost in the primary. She will not be on the ballot in November.
She did. She almost was there, though, and that’s the thing. I’m glad common sense won the day in Wisconsin, that the good people there love turkey.
I know that you say that the argument is based on how Democrats are out of touch, but we have talked about some ways in which Donald Trump has not lived up to folks’ expectations, particularly on things like prices and on things like the Iran war.
How does the GOP overcome that electability question? What is their message when folks ask, is their life better than two years ago?
I think we’ve got to lock in. I think we also need to prosecute the case that it’s going to be a lot worse under the Democrats if these crazy communists get into office. And so I think that when you’re looking at costs, we need to make that argument central. We need to make that what we lead with.

news.title: A Bayh-gone era for Indiana Democrats?
news.text:
Now it’s one of Evan Bayh’s sons, Beau Bayh, seeking office in Indiana. On Aug. 8 at Potawatomi Park in South Bend, Beau Bayh delivered a kick-out-the-bums rallying cry to regular applause from 150 or so Democratic activists and local candidates. Beau Bayh, 30, is running for Indiana’s secretary of state — seeking not only his father’s political starter job from four decades ago but also trying to resurrect the moribund Democratic brand in the Hoosier State.

It’s been 14 years since Democrats won a statewide race in Indiana. Since then, Republicans have cemented control of both Senate seats, the governor’s office, overwhelming supermajorities in the state’s House and Senate, and no less than a White House-led effort to eliminate the state’s remaining two Democratic members of Congress (which was its own source of chaotic drama). President Donald Trump won Indiana in 2024 by 59% to 40% over Democratic rival Kamala Harris. 

So, in the wilderness and under siege, the state’s remaining Democratic Party brass set their sights on Birch Evans “Beau” Bayh IV to spark something close to a renaissance. All from the office that oversees election administration and business licensing.

In other words, no pressure.

A three-way race

Speaking just off to the side from the picnic tables filled with activists, Bayh told the Washington Examiner he was called to public service by a desire to help and to clean out the corruption he said has grown in the past four years.

“I was raised in a family of public servants, and I was always taught growing up that no one forces you to run for public office, but if you decide to do that, you ought to do it to help your community, your state, and your country,” Beau Bayh said before taking the mic at the St. Joseph’s County Democrats third annual Picnic in the Park. “When I see the current secretary of state use his position of trust with the public, his office, not as it means to benefit our state, as it means to benefit himself, that kind of offends my sense of what a public servant should be.”

In any normal situation, the race would be a cakewalk for the candidate with the “R” next to their name.

But a whirlwind of state and national scandals, a chaotic intraparty Republican fight, and the emergence of a third-party wild card — as well as interviews with more than two dozen Indiana Democratic and Republican operatives over the last few months — give the impression Beau Bayh could indeed win in November. 

Indiana’s secretary of state is rarely a blockbuster race, but in the absence of a governor’s race or top-tier Senate battle, it’s the main draw. The (limited) publicly available data reveal a surprising three-way showdown between Bayh, Republican Max Engling — a former congressional aide and losing 2024 House candidate — and former Indianapolis Mayor Greg Ballard, running as an independent under the banner of his newly created Lincoln Party.

Bayh had $2.3 million in the bank at the end of June. Engling is sitting on a meager $15,000 after a late entry (more on that in a second). And Ballard has raised and spent close to $1 million, according to numbers compiled by the Indiana Capital Chronicle.

Beau Bayh looks comfortable working the crowd, talking with older Democrats long sold on the Bayh brand dating back to Birch Bayh’s time in office and younger activists with barely a memory of the Bayh family reign. 

“We need leaders here in our state that recognize that what we have in common as Americans and Hoosiers will always be more important than the little things they try and use to divide us amongst each other,” Bayh told the crowd. “I know, some folks here today might call me naive. I get it. I see this vitriol in our politics, I’m subjected to it myself, as is every brave person who’s had the courage to put their name on the ballot here this fall.”

At his back is a strong team of Indiana veterans and national Democratic operatives with Hoosier ties, including Mike Schmuhl, an architect of Pete Buttigieg’s rise from South Bend mayor with an unpronounceable last name to standout national Democratic star. 

“Beau is an excellent candidate,” said Schmuhl, a senior adviser to Beau Bayh and veteran Indiana Democratic leader. “He’s doing all the right things. He’s very disciplined. He has a professional team. He’s taking it very seriously. He’s raising the resources to win a statewide race in Indiana, something we haven’t done obviously since 2012.”

But the state’s Democratic Party infrastructure, which was built on a framework of union workers, teachers, and rural and urban coalitions, has been gutted in recent decades through a mix of factory closures, offshoring, and strategic cuts to union and teacher support by the state’s dominant Republican Party.

Coming out of the summer, Beau Bayh looks in a surprisingly strong position, but the fall homestretch appears to be a grueling battle. 

Bayh and his team built a strategy of running against the state’s unpopular incumbent Republican Secretary of State Diego Morales, who allegedly used tax dollars to buy a $90,000 GMC Yukon Denali from a dealer who donated to his campaign, traveled the globe on secret trips, and kicked up a steady storm of mini-scandals. 

Just days before the filing deadline, the state’s new GOP powerbrokers, Sen. Jim Banks (R-IN) and Attorney General Todd Rokita, called for Morales to leave the race. After he refused, they helped former congressional staffer Engling oust Morales at the state party convention.

Engling, a new Republican candidate with a clean record and strong ties in Washington and Indiana — not unlike Beau Bayh himself — entered the race late with an initial fundraising deficit. 

But all expectations are that fundraising will pick up easily for the new candidate, not least because of his strong ties to former House Speaker Kevin McCarthy, a GOP fundraising juggernaut.

Still a red state

Republicans are confident they’ll have plenty of material to blast Beau Bayh with as the fall campaign heats up, starting with what critics call Beau Bayh’s rather tenuous ties to Indiana.

Bayh was born in Indianapolis when his father was governor. After Evan Bayh was elected to the Senate in 1998, the family moved to Washington, D.C. Beau Biden graduated from St. Albans School and then Harvard College. He was then commissioned in the Marine Corps and deployed to Europe following the Russian invasion of Ukraine. He was honorably discharged at the rank of captain in 2023. 

Bayh earned a Juris Doctor from Harvard Law School and moved to Westfield, Indiana, to study for the bar exam in 2024. After passing, he clerked for a federal appeals court judge and then joined an Indianapolis law firm. 

Indiana connections to Bayh family members have already proven a political liability. Evan Bayh’s ill-fated 2016 Senate comeback bid, after six years out of office, was undone in no small part by attacks that he was too much Washington and had forgotten his Hoosier roots. This was punctuated by an Indianapolis Star investigation that showed neighbors at his Indianapolis condo rarely, if ever, saw him.

And the “carpetbagger” attack has already been primed in a tough intraparty Democratic battle in which Army veteran Blythe Potter’s supporters roundly knocked Beau Bayh as an elite Ivy League product of Washington with little connection to Indiana beyond his last name. (Beau Bayh beat Potter at the state party convention 1,385 to 883 — hardly a knockout.)

W. JAMES ANTLE: DOES ANYONE WANT TO WIN THE MIDTERM ELECTIONS?

The wild card for Beau Bayh and the GOP’s Engling, ironically, is the surprisingly well-funded third-party bid of Ballard. He was Indianapolis’s mayor from 2008 to 2016, as a Republican. He joined the secretary of state’s race as an independent amid mounting reports of corruption by Morales, the GOP incumbent. 

For Beau Bayh and the state’s Democrats seeking an institutional foothold, they’re now bracing for a flood of money for Engling and a subsequent wave of attacks in the final months of the race. 

Tom LoBianco is editor and co-founder of 24sight News, based in Silver Spring, Maryland. He is the author of the biography about President Donald Trump’s first vice president, Piety & Power: Mike Pence and the Taking of the White House, and was an Indiana statehouse reporter for the Associated Press.

news.title: NABJ says Stephen A. Smith crossed the line. What line? | Opinion
news.text:
Stephen A. Smith may be the most popular sports commentator in America. He's smart. Extremely opinionated. Loud. And he knows how to stir up fans just enough to keep them coming back for more.

He's also done what few sports commentators have been able to do: build a massive multimedia enterprise that extends far beyond simply talking about sports. Yet he has also found himself embroiled in controversy, particularly over his criticism of Black people and, more specifically, women.

His public clashes with U.S. Rep. Jasmine Crockett (D-Texas), political commentator Joy Reid, former First Lady Michelle Obama and former Vice President Kamala Harris helped land Smith on a list no Black journalist wants to make: A 2026 Thumbs Down Award from the National Association of Black Journalists. (Spoiler: I am a long-time NABJ member, but I was not involved in the award.)

NABJ uses the award, established in 1989, to call out individuals, groups and media organizations for reporting, commentary or practices the organization considers insensitive, racist, stereotypical or otherwise contrary to its mission.

I was sitting in the ballroom at NABJ's convention in Atlanta Aug. 15 when Smith's name was announced during the 2026 Salute to Excellence gala. I was there because I had been nominated for two journalism awards. Thankfully, neither was a Thumbs Down Award.

When Smith's name was called, you could feel the reaction. Some journalists sighed. Some laughed. Some clapped. Others seemed genuinely shocked.

I understood why.

Giving that distinction to Smith, a Black journalist who has supported NABJ for decades, was a slap in the face. One of the most prominent organizations of Black journalists was publicly telling one of the most prominent Black voices in media that he had crossed a line.

Opinion: Walker wins without big urban areas is a message to Crowley

Depending on where you stood, that line was either long overdue or dangerously subjective.

The award has been around since 1989, and NABJ says it has been issued 44 times to individuals and institutions. Smith said most recipients have been organizations and that he's only the seventh individual in NABJ history to receive one.

Smith also pointed out that one of those individuals was disgraced former New York Times reporter Jayson Blair, who received the award in 2003. In Smith's view, NABJ had essentially put him in the same company as a journalist whose career collapsed in one of the most notorious plagiarism and fabrication scandals in modern journalism.

Did Stephen A. Smith deserve NABJ's Thumbs Down Award?

Smith wasn't the only recipient. NABJ also gave Thumbs Down Awards to FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, CBS News, The Washington Post and DuJuan McCoy, CEO of Circle City Broadcasting.

But Smith was by far the most famous name. So how does one of the most successful Black journalists in America, a man who has supported NABJ and credits the organization with helping his career, end up receiving one of its strongest public rebukes?

The organization pointed to what it described as a pattern of disparaging commentary about prominent Black women. NABJ President Errin Haines said the organization has a responsibility to hold people accountable, regardless of how prominent or successful they are. She said the goal isn't to permanently condemn people or organizations, but to push them to do better.

And that accountability, Haines said, has to include NABJ's friends and allies. If ESPN and Smith support the organization, that shouldn't make them immune from being called out when NABJ believes they've fallen short, in this case a string of comments about Black women, including:

Criticizing Rep. Crockett for what he called “verbiage and rhetoric for the streets” and questioned whether her confrontational approach toward President Donald Trump was helping her constituents. He later apologized.Pointing to Reid's declining ratings after MSNBC canceled her show and questioning whether she should have expected a different outcome. Reid fired back, accusing Smith of being rewarded for saying things about Black people, particularly Black women, that White audiences wanted to hear.Calling out Michelle Obama over comments she made during the 2024 presidential campaign and repeatedly questioned Harris' campaign strategy.

Smith called the award a “personal hit job.” He also blasted NABJ for condemning him without first reaching out to him and giving him an opportunity to respond. He rejects the idea that criticizing prominent Black women means he is disparaging them. His criticism, he argues, has been about their words, politics and public actions, not their race or gender.

I think Smith has a point. As an opinion columnist myself, I believe NABJ went too far.

Of all the examples, Smith's criticism of Crockett troubles me the most. Describing the rhetoric of an accomplished Black congresswoman as being “for the streets” carries racial and gender implications that Smith should have understood.

But Smith also called Crockett educated and brilliant. More importantly, he apologized. That matters.

Can a Black journalist be especially tough on Black women, of Black people in general, without being accused of tearing the Black race down? And who gets to decide when tough commentary crosses that line?

Here's another question: Would Smith have received this award if the people he repeatedly criticized had been Black men?

I don't think so.

Smith goes after Black men all the time. Athletes. Coaches. Executives. Entertainers. He raises his voice, questions their decisions and sometimes says things that make them angry enough to respond publicly.

Sometimes he does go too far, but that's also Stephen A. Smith.

So, if we're going to say Smith crossed a line with Black women, NABJ should be able to show us exactly where that line is. Because criticizing a Black woman isn't the same thing as attacking all Black women.

But what about Smith's tone?

I'm not going to ignore the elephant in the room. The question isn't simply whether Smith criticizes Black women. It's whether his tone changes when he does.

Former ESPN colleague Jemele Hill believes it does. She argues that Smith doesn't always “keep the same energy,” showing more restraint with some critics while becoming much more aggressive with others.

Hill pointed to President Donald Trump as an example. After Smith criticized the disruption caused by Trump's security presence at an NBA Finals game at Madison Square Garden, Trump blasted Smith on Truth Social, calling him “dumb as a rock,” an “arrogant fool” and a “low-IQ individual.”

Yet Hill said people didn't sense the same level of vitriol from Smith toward Trump that they've seen him direct toward some Black women.

That's a fair criticism, and Smith shouldn't dismiss it. But tone is also subjective. What sounds unnecessarily harsh to one person can sound like Stephen A. being Stephen A. to someone else.

He also needs to recognize that his words carry more weight today than they did 20 years ago. He isn't just another sports commentator. He's one of the most powerful Black voices in American media.

That doesn't mean he should go easier on Black women. It means when he turns up the heat on anyone, particularly people from a community he says he cares deeply about, he should understand the impact his words can have.

NABJ believes Smith crossed the line from commentary to cruelty.

Smith wasn't in the ballroom when his name was announced. That may have been a good thing.

Opinion: Fights show we didn't listen after Sherman Park uprising

Because knowing Stephen A., had he been there, he probably would have had plenty to say about NABJ's decision.

And the president of NABJ happens to be a Black woman.

But that doesn't change where I come down.

Smith can be abrasive. He can be wrong. And, yes, sometimes he needs to check his tone.

NABJ has every right to hold Smith accountable, just as Smith has every right to criticize Crockett, Reid, Obama or Harris.

If one of the most prominent organizations of Black journalists is going to give one of the most prominent Black journalists in America an award for commentary it considers harmful to Black women, it should be able to clearly show where legitimate criticism ended and disparagement began.

Hold Smith accountable when he crosses the line. Just make sure there's actually a line before you punish him for crossing it.

You can shorthand Farage as the British version of President Donald Trump, but that would also be shortchanging him. He stands for ending illegal immigration, free enterprise, small government, scaling back net-zero environmental economic insanity, ending illegal immigration, tax cuts for lower earners, and ending illegal immigration. Economics to one side, ending the onslaught of costly illegal immigrants remains the issue most closely connected with Farage. His enemies paint him as a nativist and a bigot, hoping that Britain’s suicidal empathy, in Gad Saad’s striking term, will obliterate Farage and his Reform Party.

The Tories and the Labourites are both in thrall to the radical elements in their parties, which means that they are culturally out of step with average citizens, who are sick and tired of the nation catering to the cost and criminality of illegal immigrants instead of caring for its poorest and weakest.

Farage’s approach comes as balm to British voters who feel betrayed and embarrassed by their dysfunctional national politics. Case in point: A U.K. citizen was recently stabbed to death by an illegal immigrant, and yet the police put handcuffs on the dying victim while the murderer went free. Events like these rightly disgust the British, which is why the nation is poised to make Farage prime minister in the next general election, no more than three years hence.

How undemocratic is the U.K. these days? Consider that the newest occupant of 10 Downing Street, former Greater Manchester Mayor Andy Burnham, won his seat in Parliament this summer with less than 25,000 votes and was promptly installed as prime minister, replacing the well-meaning but politically inept Keir Starmer. No one was allowed to run against Burnham — shades of Kamala Harris. His not-quite-14,000-vote plurality made Burnham the leader of a nation of 70 million. He was essentially chosen by a miniscule 0.05% of registered U.K. voters. Where’s the democracy in that?

Burnham intends to run the U.K. on the same woke terms as his multitudinous predecessors, which means that it’s only a matter of time before the circular firing squad that is Britain’s Labour Party scuppers him, too, which means Farage’s time is almost here. He has the Trump-like, magical ability to appeal to regular joes, but without much of the Trumpian baggage. He wears his well-spoken everyman identity lightly, still enjoying a pint, a smoke, and a good time.

Like Trump, Farage grew up in upper-middle-class comfort. He became a trader in London’s financial world instead of going to college. He became a member of the European Parliament, disgusted with the continent’s swooning over socialism, radical environmentalism, open borders, and all the mayhem those stances have caused.

Hence his championing of Brexit, which opponents deride as anti-immigration bigotry. The truth is more nuanced. It’s actually about the U.K. declaring economic independence from its Eurosclerotic neighbors and managing its economy and borders as it sees fit, instead of taking orders from unelected Eurocrats in Strasbourg and Brussels.

Farage’s Reform Party is poised to run away with the next general election. Woke outlets such as the BBC and the Guardian point to polls that show Reform losing its sway, but don’t believe the bias. The financial gift is just so much more sand in the gears from those who would silence Farage and maintain the status quo.

As the expression says, “There will always be an England.” Yet unless and until Farage takes over, don’t be so sure.

news.title: Medicare for All is back on the ballot
news.text:
Medicare for All is not simply a proposal to let more people buy into Medicare. The current Senate bill, sponsored by Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT), would create a federal health plan covering every American, eliminate premiums and cost-sharing, and make it unlawful for existing private and employer plans to exist. Medicare, Medicaid, and the Obamacare exchanges would largely be folded into the new system.

The price tag would be enormous. A 2024 Center for Health and Economy analysis estimated that Kamala Harris’s version of Medicare for All would increase federal spending by $43.9 trillion from 2026 through 2035, while CBO has separately found that similar single-payer systems would dramatically shift health spending onto the federal budget. Meanwhile, the existing Medicare program is projected to exhaust its Hospital Insurance Trust Fund reserves in 2033.

Supporters answer that Americans would no longer pay private premiums. True, but replacing premiums with taxes does not make healthcare free. The federal government would become responsible for financing the entire system.

That is an important caveat to polling. Reuters polling found this month that 60% of independents support “government-provided healthcare.” But that wording does not tell voters what Sanders’s proposal means. Under Medicare for All, Americans could not simply keep their employer plan if they preferred it. Duplicative private insurance would be illegal. Washington would not merely compete with private insurance; it would replace it.

Once government becomes the healthcare monopolist, controlling spending means controlling what providers are paid and, ultimately, how much care is supplied. CBO has found that lower provider payments are the principal source of single-payer savings and warns that increased demand would exceed increased supply, producing “delays and forgone care.”

Britain and Canada show what that reality looks like. England’s National Health Service had over 7 million cases awaiting elective treatment in June, with more than a third waiting longer than 18 weeks and more than 105,000 waiting over a year.

Canada fares little better. In an international survey, 58% of Canadians needing elective surgery waited at least two months, compared with 26% of Americans. Those who can afford to escape sometimes do: One study estimates more than 105,000 Canadians traveled abroad for nonemergency medical care in 2025.

Americans do not need to speculate about whether politicians will accept the taxes needed to build such a system. Vermont already tried. Back in 2014, Democratic Gov. Peter Shumlin abandoned Green Mountain Care after his administration concluded that financing it would require an 11.5% payroll tax and an income-based charge of up to 9.5%, warning that the “risk of economic shock” was too high.

California has reached the same conclusion in practice. Democrats have controlled the governor’s mansion since 2011 and have had supermajorities in both legislative chambers since 2018, yet they have failed to advance single-payer healthcare even to a floor vote.

If Medicare for All is such an obvious bargain, reducing costs while preserving quality without taxing the middle class, then why have Sanders’s Vermont and Rep. Ro Khanna’s (D-CA) California refused to enact it?

The reason is simple: Once Medicare for All stops being an empty promise and becomes a real plan with higher spending, lower provider pay, higher taxes, and rationed care, support for it, even in overwhelmingly Democratic states, collapses.

Self-identified socialist Democratic candidates are putting Medicare for All back on the ballot. Republicans should make sure voters understand that this means trillions in new federal spending, sweeping new taxes, the elimination of existing private coverage, and a government monopoly with the power to ration care. Democrats running this fall should answer for it.
news.summary: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY) may have refused to commit to bringing Medicare for All to a vote and distanced himself from his own past support of socializing the entire healthcare sector of the economy, but candidates winning Democratic Party primaries across the country are not as shy.
