news.title: From Booker-listed Marlon James to a memoir by Michael Douglas – the biggest books this autumn
news.text:
The Disappearers by Marlon JamesHamish Hamilton, 3 September
 After a detour into mythic fantasy, the author of the Booker-winning A Brief History of Seven Killings returns to Jamaica. This account of a brutal homophobic attack on a group of gay actors in 1980s Kingston has already been longlisted for this year’s prize.

The Bridge by Colm TóibínPicador, 3 September
 Twenty years on, this short novel is a sequel to Tóibín’s exquisite story A Long Winter, set around a family tragedy in the isolated Pyrenees. Now the building of a bridge brings modernity, possibility and threat to a father and son, in a spare chronicle of longing and grief.

The Golden Hours by Louisa YoungMantle, 3 September
 Young continues her aunt Elizabeth Jane Howard’s much-loved Cazalet Chronicles, bringing her story of a sprawling upper-middle-class English family into the swinging 60s.

Switzy by Emma ClineChatto & Windus, 10 September
 With dementia making him increasingly confused, David is on his way to a clinic in Zurich to end his life while he still has the capacity to make a choice. Longlisted for the Booker prize, this is a bravura portrait of a failing mind, told from the inside.

The Rouse by China MiévillePicador, 17 September
 A leading light of the New Weird, Miéville has been working on this stonking 1,000-page supernatural fantasy for two decades. Political intrigue, continent-hopping global conspiracy and uncanny mysteries unfold.

The Housekeeper by Rose TremainChatto & Windus, 17 September
 An origin story for Daphne du Maurier’s enduring bestseller Rebecca is told from the perspective of the novelist’s secret lover Danni, housekeeper in a Cornish mansion, who is outraged to find herself recast on the page as the malevolent Mrs Danvers.

Stations by Louise KennedyBloomsbury, 24 September
 The author of bestselling 2022 debut novel Trespasses, a Troubles-set love story recently adapted into a C4 drama starring Gillian Anderson, returns with a tale of friendship and loss. Róisín and Red meet in small-town Ireland in the 1980s and reconnect in a London squat, before Red is caught up in a cycle of poverty and addiction.

Doom Painting by AK BlakemoreGranta, 24 September
 One of our most exciting historical novelists takes on the peasants’ revolt, in a blow-by-blow account of unlikely leader Wat Tyler and the 16 days in 1381 that turned England upside down. With cinematic action and a relish for medieval vocabulary, it’s a punky successor to Hilary Mantel.

American Hagwon by Min Jin Lee
 4th Estate, 29 September
 The hagwon or cram school is a symbol of Korea’s stress on education. This new saga from the Pachinko author follows a middle-class family, their life in ruins after the 1997 Asian financial crisis, who move to Sydney and then California in search of a better future for their children.

Partita by Barbara KingsolverFaber, 6 October
 After the Pulitzer-winning Demon Copperhead, a retelling of David Copperfield set in Appalachia, Kingsolver returns with a quieter tale of midlife longing and regret. A gifted pianist, Livia used music to escape the sadness of her family life in rural Tennessee, but having married and resettled in her home town, an unexpected call from a former lover drags her back into the past.

Life Out of Order by Audrey NiffeneggerJonathan Cape, 13 October
 Set a quarter of a century on, this long-awaited sequel focuses on the daughter of the couple in The Time Traveler’s Wife. Alba has inherited her father’s extraordinary condition, jumping unpredictably across the decades, from a United States in turmoil to a dystopian future London. She’s torn between two lovers – one anchored in the present, and one a time traveller like herself.

Peck & Peck by Bonnie GarmusManilla, 13 October
 In the follow-up to global bestseller Lessons in Chemistry, it’s 1982 New York and young Batter Gray lands a job at the eponymous poetry periodical, run by feuding twin brothers. Expect charm, quirk and literary rabbit holes.

In One Brief Moment All Eternity by Elif ShafakViking, 15 October
 From the Booker and Women’s prize-shortlisted author, a study of French writer Gustave Flaubert refracted through the lives of the women around him, including his most iconic creation: Madame Bovary.

Music Against the Night by Yiyun Li
 4th Estate, 22 October
 Set at the end of the 18th century, against a background of global tumult, the Pulitzer winner’s historical epic is inspired by the lives of two musicians: Adelaide Percheron, born in French India, and the Irish John Field, the inventor of the nocturne, who will be brought together by love and talent.

Lessons in Harmony by Jonathan CoeViking, 12 November
 Music is in the air this autumn: Coe’s latest follows the friendship between French dandy Maurice Ravel and English traditionalist Ralph Vaughan Williams, exploring creativity and national identity against the encroaching shadow of the first world war.

Crime and thrillers

Sherlock Holmes, Miss Marple and George Smiley return

Autumn is back-to-school season for series authors, with William Boyd on the third of his cold war espionage novels starring travel writer Gabriel Dax. In Cold Sunset (Viking, 3 September) our reluctant spy is on his way to Russia, to tussle with the KGB. Richard Osman serves up number two in his We Solve Murders franchise: We Chase Shadows (Viking, 10 September) sees Steve, Amy and Rosie – retired cop, private security officer and bestselling crime author respectively – investigate after a body is found in the Italian hills. Five years on, Janice Hallett publishes a sequel to her hit am-dram debut The Appeal, as the Fairway Players’ new production of Agatha Christie leads to murder in The Silent Appeal (Viper, 3 September). The vigorous afterlife of the queen of crime continues elsewhere, with the first official new outing for Miss Marple, Murder at the Grand Alpine Hotel by Lucy Foley (HarperCollins, 22 September). A varied cast list, death on the mountaintop and plenty of suspects are guaranteed.

Ian Rankin, known for his grumpy Edinburgh detective John Rebus, takes a new direction in The Heights (Orion, 8 October), a standalone thriller set in a luxurious central London high-rise. And there’s a return to the world of John le Carré’s Circus in the latest from his son Nick Harkaway: in The Taper Man (Viking, 5 November), George Smiley finds himself navigating the unlikely terrain of 1960s LA in search of a communist sleeper agent.

Finally, a festive treat: 10 new adventures for the world’s most famous detective in short story anthology Sherlock (Simon & Schuster, 5 November), with contributors including Sarah Perry, Joe Hill, Abir Mukherjee and Kate Mosse.

Swan Song: Diana, My Sister by Charles Spencer Penguin Michael Joseph, 22 September
 Thirty years after Princess Diana was killed in a car crash, her brother – whose euology at her funeral echoed around the world – tells the story of their upbringing and recounts the devastating week of her death.

The Castle by Jon Ronson Viking, 20 August
 A concerning late-night call from his teenage son marks the start of a strange journey into modern masculinity for the journalist and author of The Psychopath Test and So You’ve Been Publicly Shamed.

The Future Starts With Us by Gordon BrownSimon & Schuster, 1 September
 The former PM tries to join the dots between two seemingly disparate political phenomena: the erosion of the international rules-based order, exacerbated by war and climate breakdown, and the fragmentation of the tight-knit communities that keep us connected at a local level.

The Great Dictator: A Life of Barbara Cartland by Matthew Sweet Hodder & Stoughton, 10 September
 The queen of romance novels wrote a scarcely believable 723 of them during her career – with a little help from an amanuensis or two. Historian Sweet tells the extraordinary story of a woman born into an upper‑middle-class family fallen on hard times, who navigated scandal and opprobrium to become one of the bestselling writers of the 20th century.

Queens and Kings: An Unusually Personal History by Lucy Worsley Hodder & Stoughton, 3 September 
 The historian and chief curator of royal palaces brings a personal touch to some of British history’s pivotal moments, focusing on the places in which they unfolded, and in which Worsley herself has worked: Hampton Court, Kensington Palace and the Tower of London.

All the Wrong Moves by Anthony Scaramucci Bodley Head, 17 September
 Not many political figures are able to give Liz Truss a run for her money in the shortest-ever-tenure stakes, but Scaramucci, Trump’s press secretary for just 10 days, is one of them. Since then he’s reinvented himself as one of the administration’s sharpest critics. His first book is an attempt to chart how the US went from stable postwar consensus to today’s “shitshow politics”.

End Times Fascism by Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor Allen Lane, 15 September
 Thinkers and activists Klein and Taylor have identified a distinctive strand of rightwing nihilism: the kind that seeks to reshape the world in its image, even as it devours the natural resources on which our survival depends (certain tech barons and authoritarian leaders may feel particularly seen). Here they offer both a diagnosis and a plan for resistance.

Profits, Prophets, Coaches and Kings: (When) Do Leaders Make a Difference? by Jared Diamond Mariner, 22 September
 The author of Guns, Germs and Steel, known for his analyses of the grand, impersonal forces that shape human destiny, returns with a timely book on the role of prominent individuals. What difference does a sports coach, a CEO or an erratic president really make to the fortunes of teams, companies and global civilisation?

An Unexpected Life: A Memoir by Gloria Steinem Ebury, 22 September
 A totemic figure in American feminism, Steinem sought to carry the momentum of the civil rights era into what became known as the women’s liberation movement. Here she writes about her childhood and political awakening, and reflects from the present moment on nearly 60 years of activism.

Hawking: His Life and Work by Graham FarmeloJohn Murray, 24 September
 In the first authorised biography of Stephen Hawking, Farmelo paints an intimate portrait of the acclaimed physicist based on unique access to his diaries and letters, as well as interviews with family and close associates.

The American Way of Killing: The Invention of an Epidemic by Malcolm GladwellAbacus, 29 September
 The author of The Tipping Point asks why the United States has ended up being so much more violent than comparable countries around the world. From a Chicago ER to a 17th-century court case, he explores stories that may hold the key to what he describes as “the most pressing of all American social problems”.

Blockers: Rebels in the Deep State by Michael Lewis Allen Lane, 6 October
 Lewis’s pacy, high-stakes nonfiction has been drawing readers since 1989’s Liar’s Poker, an account of his time on Wall Street in the 1980s. Here he deploys his powers of narration to tell the story of how the US Department of Government Efficiency (Doge) sought to dismantle the state – though his real subject is the principled civil servants who stood in the way of Elon Musk’s campaign of vandalism.

Requiem for Gaza by Joe Sacco and Chris Hedges Jonathan Cape, 8 October 
 The master of graphic reportage and author of Palestine teams up with veteran war correspondent Hedges to document the devastating Israeli war on Gaza and its human impact. Interviewing 29 displaced Palestinian families, Sacco and Hedges tell stories of death, destruction and resilience.

The Perilous Fight by Colin KaepernickGrand Central Publishing, 8 October
 The NFL quarterback made history in 2016 when he knelt for the US national anthem, rather than standing. Since that time, “taking the knee” has become an emblem of the fight for racial justice, in the US and beyond. In his memoir, Kaepernick traces the relationships and experiences that culminated in a pivotal sporting and political moment.

Promise Me, America by Joe BidenJohn Murray, 17 November
 A year on from 107 Days, in which former vice-president Kamala Harris detailed her boss’s failure to get out of the way, Joe Biden tells his side of the story in a book which promises to reveal “the deeply agonising calculation behind his decision … to step aside from the presidential race”.

Pay Attention by Laura KuenssbergCorsair, 5 November 
 The former BBC political editor’s first book reflects on 20 years of upheaval in British politics, and what the broadcaster perceives as being at the root of it all: a failure by the political class to really listen to what people have actually been saying.

Holding Lightning: The Life, Loves and Art of Whitney Houston by Emily LordiWhite Rabbit, 1 October
 English professor Lordi treats the career of one of pop’s greatest stars with the seriousness it deserves, but with emotional intelligence too, tracing the arc of Houston’s life from global success to personal tragedy.

From Hollywood hijinks to political scandal – life stories to look out for

It’s another bumper autumn for Hollywood stars with plenty of tales to tell – though this year skews male. Michael Douglas’s One Helluva Ride (Headline, 6 October) includes details of “affairs with some of the most celebrated actresses in Hollywood” and the “serious drug addiction that threatened to destroy his first marriage and career”. If you’re still in the mood for testosterone-laced hijinks after that, there’s Sylvester Stallone’s The Steps (Seven Dials, 29 September), which charts the Rocky star’s 1970s journey from homelessness to the Oscars. For a more multilayered take on acting and fame, try Fictional Selves by Kyle MacLachlan (Century, 29 September), whose talent in picking idiosyncratic roles such as such as Agent Cooper in Twin Peaks has earned him a cult following. And then there’s screen icon Dustin Hoffman, whose first memoir Look at Me (Gallery, 10 November), published as he prepares to enter his 10th decade, covers the pressures of being dubbed the “voice of a generation” after The Graduate, and his many acting roles since that extraordinary breakthrough. It would make a neat pairing with Watergate reporter Bob Woodward’s memoir Secrets (Simon & Schuster, 24 November): that era-defining scoop was dramatised in All the President’s Men, with Hoffman playing Woodward’s partner, Carl Bernstein.

On the other side of the Atlantic, Judi Dench reminisces about a 70-year career in Is It Too Late to Make a Run for It? (Michael Joseph, 22 October). In Vigilauntie (W&N, 3 September) actor and co-creator of the groundbreaking sketch show Goodness Gracious Me, Meera Syal, writes about family, frustration and making it as an Asian woman on TV, while another veteran of the small screen, Russell T Davies, charts a writing career that has spanned Coronation Street and Doctor Who in The Queerest of Folk (Bantam, 8 October). Everyone’s favourite communist standup Alexei Sayle gets political in How I’ve Tried to Change the World (W&N, 3 September), a memoir of protest through the decades, while actual politician and scourge of the BNP in her Barking constituency, Margaret Hodge, shares the lessons of a life on the frontlines in Battle Axe (William Collins, 10 September).
news.summary:
Midlife meditations from Barbara Kingsolver; musical portraits by Jonathan Coe and Yiyun Li; plus memoirs from Dustin Hoffman and Judi Dench – all among the coming season’s highlights

news.title: On This Day, Aug. 22: IRA founder Michael Collins assassinated
news.text:
Aug. 22 (UPI) -- On this date in history:

In 1851, the U.S.-built schooner America outran a fleet of Britain's finest ships around England's Isle of Wight in an international race that became known as the America's Cup.

In 1881, American humanitarians Clara Barton and Adolphus Solomons founded the National Red Cross.

In 1922, Michael Collins, a founder of the Irish Republican Army and a key figure in Ireland's independence movement, was assassinated by political opponents.

In 1968, Pope Paul VI arrived in Colombia, becoming the first pontiff to visit South America.

In 1986, Kerr-McGee Corp. agreed to pay the estate of nuclear industry worker Karen Silkwood more than $1 million, ending a 10-year legal battle waged by her family over her exposure to radioactive materials at the company's Oklahoma plant.

In 2004, two masked robbers stole Edvard Munch's The Scream and another painting from the Munch Museum in Oslo, Norway. They were found about two years later and put back on display in 2008. The Scream had been stolen once before, 10 years earlier, but was recovered within three months.

In 2005, the last Jewish settlers moved peacefully out of the Gaza Strip after carrying Torah scrolls down the main street of Netzarim, last of 21 settlements to be evacuated.

In 2006, Pulkovo Airlines Flight 612 crashed near the Russian border in Ukraine, killing 171 people.

In 2011, the Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. National Memorial in Washington opened to the public. The $120 million memorial, 25 years in the making, is on a four-acre site on the National Mall.

In 2017, India's Supreme Court declared the "instant divorce" practice among the nation's Muslim population to be unconstitutional.

In 2021, Vice President Kamala Harris visited Singapore, her first visit to Asia as VP, to discuss issues of climate change, the COVID-19 pandemic and supply chain concerns with Singapore Prime Minister Lee Shien Loong.
news.summary: On Aug. 22, 1922, Michael Collins, a founder of the Irish Republican Army and a key figure in Ireland's independence movement, was assassinated.

news.title: How 35-year-old Natalie Harp Became Donald Trump's Favorite Assistant
news.text:
In recent years, few people in US President Donald Trump's entourage have appeared beside him as frequently as his assistant, 35-year-old Natalie Harp, reports the BBC.

Natalie Harp is one of Trump's long-standing and most loyal aides.

This week, she once again found herself in the spotlight due to statements made by Trump's opponent, Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff of Georgia. The politician unleashed a new wave of criticism on Trump and mentioned Natalie Harp in his speech, which widely circulated on social media.

Criticizing the president, Ossoff stated:

“He [Trump] doesn’t want to do his job. He wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie on what appears to be their entirely defenseless flying palace, gifted by the Emir of Qatar.”

 The senator was referring to the new presidential aircraft Air Force One ("Aircraft One"), as well as journalists' reports that Harp likely flew with Trump on a secret flight from Turkey after the NATO summit. 

Earlier, the American press reported that Trump, upon departing from Ankara in early July, used an in-flight catering van to discreetly transfer from "Aircraft One" to "Aircraft Two." The secret flight, as reported by the media, was linked to an alleged threat from Iran.

Cancer and an Unusual Path to the White House

Natalie Harp was born in California to a Christian family with conservative views. Her path to the White House can be described as atypical.

 She became known for crediting Trump with saving her life. 

During his first term, Trump pushed for the passage of the Right to Try Act, which gave patients broader access to experimental treatments. Harp was then able to use this opportunity to receive treatment for bone cancer using experimental methods, as traditional chemotherapy had not yielded positive results in her case.

“When the available chemotherapy didn't work, nobody wanted to take me for clinical trials […] They didn't give me the right to try experimental treatments, Mr. President. You did, and without you, I would have died waiting for their permission,” she said at the 2020 Republican National Convention.

 After the event, Trump said that Natalie Harp, with her appearance, "lit up the television screen like few" he had ever seen. 

Natalie Harp, who frequently spoke about her treatment experience and expressed gratitude to Trump, was quickly recognized within the MAGA ("Make America Great Again") wing of the Republican Party.

Soon after, she joined the campaign's advisory board during Trump's 2020 election campaign.

"Trump's Biggest Supporter"

After Trump's defeat in the 2020 election, Harp became a host on the right-wing conservative cable news channel One America News Network (OAN).

There, she became known as a staunch defender of Donald Trump, also claiming that he had allegedly won the 2020 election.

She left the TV channel in 2022 to join Trump's next presidential campaign.

Most information regarding Trump's relationship with Harp comes from anonymous sources, mentioned in books by journalists such as Maggie Haberman, Jonathan Swan, or Michael Wolff. Almost nothing is known about Natalie Harp's personal life.

Her brother, Preston Harp, explained his sister's unusual devotion to Trump in a CNN interview by saying that the current president embodies everything their mother taught them to respect in life.

“That’s why I think, honestly, her fascination with Trump comes from there,” Preston Harp said.

He added that Harp had been obsessed with the idea of working in the White House since she was young and had written letters to previous presidents, including George W. Bush during the Iraq War.

In a CNN interview, Harp's brother said that her “dream finally came true” when she got into the White House, and that his sister was “Trump’s biggest supporter, so he probably likes her.”

 “She’s beautiful, she has a good character. She thinks he saved her life, so a person for whom such gratitude is felt must feel very good about it,” he said. 

Harp's official position at the White House is Executive Assistant to the President, a role not typically high-level, involving managing logistics, scheduling, and communication flow.

However, it appears Harp has given this role new meaning, and her authority is significantly higher than that of her predecessors, such as Madeleine Westerhout in Trump's first administration.

What Influence Does Natalie Harp Have on Trump?

When CNN reporter Kristen Holmes asked Trump this week about Ossoff’s comments, the US president lashed out at her with criticism. “You’re being very disrespectful… Fake news, you’re fake news […] You’re a fake journalist and you report fake news,” Trump reacted to the reporter’s question.

The White House later published a video recording of Trump’s conversation with the journalist on its official X page, accusing her of using a “cheap” and crude tactic in her work.

“One day your children will learn about your disgusting and inhumane question. They will be uncomfortable and ashamed to see a parent display such heartlessness,” another post addressed to Holmes stated.

Trump's aide, Natalie Harp, is almost inseparable from President Donald Trump during his second term.

 Reporters at the White House often see her just steps away from Trump in the Oval Office or aboard Air Force One during many of his domestic and international trips. 

“She’s always there. Literally always,” a source close to the White House told the BBC.

Among those close to the White House and press representatives, she is often called a "living printer," as she is frequently seen with a portable printer, which she needs to print articles and social media posts for Trump on paper — because he prefers to read publications on paper.

This means that Harp likely has significant opportunities to control exactly what information and messages Trump receives, notes another source familiar with White House operations.

Other anonymous sources described her to American media as the president's "gatekeeper" and "favorite toy."

Harp also acts as a kind of social media secretary for Trump: she posts messages on his Truth Social account on his behalf.

In one video that widely circulated on social media after Ossoff’s comments, Harp is captured typing text for social media at Trump’s dictation, as he watches Kamala Harris’s 2024 speech.

Amid recent attention on Harp, the White House stated that she is a “trusted and valuable” member of the team, though Trump himself has rarely spoken about her on camera.

Ossoff was one of many Trump critics who noted that Harp was reportedly on board the plane on which the president departed from Turkey after the US allegedly received intelligence about a threat from Iran.

 When journalist Maggie Haberman, who has written extensively and continues to write about Trump's presidency, was asked during an interview why Trump took Harp with him on "Aircraft Two" when departing from Turkey on a secret flight, she replied: "Because for him, if one can put it this way, she's like a pacifier, like a favorite warm blanket, a favorite toy — in short, something that creates a feeling of comfort and peace."
Haberman and Jonathan Swan reported in a 2024 New York Times publication that Harp allegedly wrote in a letter to Trump: "You are everything that matters to me."

news.title: Trump says he would be happy if allowed to run for third presidential term
news.text:
WASHINGTON, August 22. /TASS/. US President Donald Trump said he would be happy if the country's laws were changed to allow him to run for a third term as head of state.

"We have rules and regulation that says you're not allowed to run. If they'd like to change that, be very happy," Trump told supporters in Myrtle Beach, South Carolina.

By law, Trump's second term as president is scheduled to end in January 2029. The 22nd Amendment to the US Constitution, adopted in 1951, limits a president to two terms in office. However, the current American leader has repeatedly raised the possibility of seeking reelection to a third term.

Trump won the presidency for a second time in November 2024, defeating Democratic candidate Kamala Harris. He previously served his first term from 2017 to 2021.
news.summary: Donald Trump won the presidency for a second time in November 2024, defeating Democratic candidate Kamala Harris

news.title: US VP Vance campaigns in hometown with eye on 2028
news.text:
US vice-president JD Vance said the Trump administration is 'making progress' on issues including 'the affordability question' amid anger over rising prices. (EPA Images pic)
MIDDLETOWN: US vice-president JD Vance returned to his hometown Friday to campaign for Republicans in November's crucial midterm elections - and test his own hopes of succeeding Donald Trump in 2028.
Vance gave a speech at the steel plant where his grandfather worked for 40 years in Middletown, Ohio, the blue-collar town which featured in his bestselling 2016 memoir "Hillbilly Elegy".
The book recounted an impoverished upbringing in the neglected rust belt that spawned Trump's "Make America Great Again" movement, which Vance needs to woo if he runs for the White House in two years.
But Vance is also seeking to boost Republican candidates ahead of the midterms, amid fears that Trump's unpopularity could cause the party to lose control of Congress.
Trump's approval rating has fallen to 33 percent, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted last week, the lowest of his current term.
Vance took a subtly centrist tone in his speech, evoking his blue-collar upbringing while avoiding much of the harsh rhetoric that has made Trump so divisive.
"I remember my papaw... coming to this very place to work for nearly 40 years as a welder," Vance said.
The isolationist vice-president, who has privately opposed Trump's Iran war, said his grandfather had "very simple" expectations including that "America never be asked to be the policeman of the world".
Vance added that the Trump administration was "making progress" on issues including "the affordability question". Voters have voiced anger over rising prices, which his boss has dismissed as a hoax launched by rival Democrats.
But the 42-year-old also had harsh words for the opposition on subjects including immigration and so-called "woke" politics.
Urging Republicans to vote in November, he said: "Get out there and fight for yourself by telling the far-left radicals who have taken over the Democratic Party: 'This is not your country. It's our country, and we're going to fight for it.'"
The race to succeed Trump in 2028 - assuming he does not try for a constitutionally barred third term - is set to begin in earnest after the midterms.
Vance has declined to formally confirm that he will run but has been clearly positioning himself as the heir to Trump's MAGA movement, albeit without the rough edges.
But many in the Republican party are also looking at US secretary of state Marco Rubio as a contender.
Rubio has said he will not run if Vance does, but a poll by Emerson College and The Hill released this week found that Rubio outperformed Vance in all but one of five match-ups against leading Democratic contenders.
The Democrats meanwhile face their own struggles as they seek to rebuild from Trump's 2024 defeat of then-vice-president Kamala Harris.
The far-left wing of the Democratic Party has scored a series of primary wins in recent months, even as centrists seek to distance themselves from socialist-style proposals like universal health care.
news.summary: JD Vance is also seeking to boost Republican candidates ahead of November's midterm elections amid fears the party could lose control of Congress.

news.title: Whatley Within Striking Distance of Defeating Roy Cooper in North Carolina
news.text: Republican Michael Whatley is within striking distance of former Democratic Governor Roy Cooper in the race for North Carolina’s open U.S. Senate seat, according to a new High Point University poll released Friday. The race is for the seat currently held by Republican Senator Thom Tillis, who is not seeking reelection. Cooper, who served as North Carolina governor from 2017 through 2024, is seeking a return to elected office, while Whatley is the former chairman of the Republican National Committee (RNC) and the North Carolina Republican Party. Jeff Allen, Cooper for North Carolina campaign manager, told Newsweek via email on Friday when asked about the new poll, "Roy Cooper has spent his career putting North Carolinians first, while Washington, D.C., insider Michael Whatley spent his delivering for billionaires and special interests at the expense of the middle class. A Democrat has not won statewide federal office in North Carolina in nearly two decades and we know this race will be very close, which is why we’re building a campaign to earn every vote and make sure North Carolinians know that Roy Cooper will fight for them in the Senate." Newsweek also reached out to Whatley's campaign via email on Friday for comment. Why It Matters Republicans in the Senate hold a 53-45 majority—excluding independent Senators Bernie Sanders and Angus King, who caucus with Democrats—and Democrats view flipping the seat as a potential pathway to taking control of the upper chamber. Midterm elections are also commonly seen as a measure of public approval for the current president too, and the president's party has traditionally lost seats during these elections. Trump has backed Whatley in the race, adding another layer of potential intensity. What To Know The contest is viewed as one of the key Senate races of the 2026 midterms, with the outcome potentially affecting control of the chamber. The Cook Political Report has the race slated as Lean Democrat. The poll showed that among likely voters, Cooper leads Whatley 50 percent to 45 percent, a 5-point advantage that falls within the poll’s 5.2-percentage-point credibility interval. The poll shows that 3 percent are unsure or would not vote and 3 percent would pick someone else or another party. The survey of 800 self-identified registered voters, including 660 likely voters, was conducted August 3-12. The poll marks a closer contest than some recent surveys have suggested. Among all self-identified registered voters, Cooper leads Whatley 48 percent to 41 percent, with 8 percent unsure or saying they would not vote and 4 percent saying they would pick someone else or another party. The HPU poll gives that group a 4.3-percentage-point credibility interval. Grant Reeher, professor of political science at Syracuse University, told Newsweek via email on Friday in part, "One has to be careful about slicing the results too thin. It was also an online poll, as I understand it. I’d be wary of investing too much meaning in a couple point shift from previous polls when the margin of error is 5 points." "But having said all that," Reeher added, "a smallish shift is not surprising, given the recent unpopularity of the Iran War, and persistent inflation and interest rate concerns. It’s still anyone’s race, even though I agree with Cook that it looks like it’s leaning toward the Dems. And Cooper may not have as much of the negativity associated with the Democratic brand as some other candidates." D. Stephen Voss, political science professor at the University of Kentucky, also told Newsweek via email on Friday: "The tightening of the North Carolina race makes sense because of the name-recognition advantage Roy Cooper enjoyed going into the contest. Likely voters knew him and many knew they were ready to support him. Fewer voters knew Michael Whatley, reporting neither a favorable nor an unfavorable opinion of him. "It makes sense that as the race gained more attention, the sort of people who typically vote Republican would be returning to the fold, leaving fewer likely voters still unsure of what they'll do. That's the educational function that election season performs. Once Whatley finishes picking up the voters who always should have been his, though, persuading the remainder will become just as hard for him as it is for Cooper," Voss concluded. The HPU poll points to a challenging political environment for Republicans in the state. Among likely voters, 59 percent say the country is on the wrong track, compared with 36 percent who say it is headed in the right direction. Trump’s approval rating stands at 42 percent, with 54 percent disapproving, while 48 percent of likely voters say North Carolina itself was on the wrong track. Those broader numbers could give Cooper an advantage, but Whatley’s five-point deficit among likely voters is close enough that the race remains competitive with less than three months until Election Day. Trump won the swing state in the 2024 presidential election versus former Vice President Kamala Harris by 3.3 percent. What Other Polls Show Other recent polling has generally shown Cooper with a larger advantage. An Elon University poll released earlier this month found Cooper ahead of Whatley 53 percent to 42 percent among likely voters. The poll surveyed 800 North Carolina adults from July 23 to July 31, 2026, and has a margin of error of 5.6 percent for likely voters. A Carolina Journal Poll shows Cooper leading with 51.5 percent to Whatley's 39 percent. The survey, conducted by Harper Polling, was from August 9 to August 10, 2026, and has a margin of error of 4 percent.
